disciplines.name: Context engineering
disciplines.question: When the agent starts work, does it already know what it needs (and nothing it doesn't), without you carrying it in each time?
disciplines.scope_note: Everything the agent works from: rules, project facts, docs, notes, tool definitions and the session itself. Also how all of it stays right as sessions grow, end and restart, and as the work spreads to a team. Context is any knowledge the agent works from, not only facts about the project (ruling 10). 'Context engineering' is the name of the discipline, and 'write, select, compress, isolate' names its four buckets. Neither is a practice. Write = rules and notes kept outside the session (write-down-what-it-cannot-know, notes-the-next-chat-reads). Select = load only where it applies, fetch when needed (put-rules-where-they-apply, let-the-agent-fetch). Compress = compact and trim (compact-on-purpose, keep-always-loaded-small). Isolate = sub-agents and fresh sessions (isolate-side-work, reset-with-a-handoff). Prompt bloat and instruction stacking live here, not in prompt, because they are about what loads every turn. Outside this discipline: the ask itself and goal drift (prompt), whether the work is right (verification), permissions and guardrails (harness), several agents at once and work that runs without the person (orchestration). Hooks are a technique here, not a practice. The Level 2 to Level 3 border runs through this discipline: who carries the context. Either the person does, session by session (L2), or a setup they engineered does (L3). Every level is checked the same way: a fresh session that never saw the conversation shows what reached it. The automated form of that check, evals the agent can't edit, lives in verification.

disciplines.name: Prompt engineering
disciplines.question: How do you hand work to the agent: the task, the approach, and the words you use when it misses?
disciplines.scope_note: This discipline covers how work is handed over and the words used for it: the task, the approach agreed before any code, what finished looks like, how a miss is corrected, and the prompts a person keeps and reuses (saved prompts, skills, commands and sub-agent instructions they wrote). The vocabulary files goal drift under context; it is drafted here because most of its fix is in the hand-over. Out of scope: what loads into every session (prompt bloat and instruction stacking go to context), checking the result (verification), and running many agents (orchestration). Four terms are dropped as model-level because a person can't fix them: majority label / recency / common token bias, alignment tax, exaggerated safety, and lobotomized (model). His 10-27 ruling sets the tone: 'everybody plans work… our focus shouldn't be on plan driven strategies'. So no practice here reads a level from planning or plan mode alone.

disciplines.name: Verification and evals
disciplines.question: How do you know the agent's work is right before it counts, and who can explain what shipped?
disciplines.scope_note: Covers how the agent's output gets checked: proof the agent has to show, a second look from a reviewer that didn't write the work, the person reading and owning what ships. It also covers testing your own agent setup (prompts, rules, skills, sub-agents) with evals. Comprehension debt, automation bias, AI slop, vibe coding, cognitive surrender, skill atrophy and the 70% problem come from the vocabulary's 'human' family. They live here because the fix for them lives here. Not here: agreeing the plan and sizing the task (prompt), making a correction stick in the rules (context), what the agent may reach and the guardrails around it (harness; hooks show up here only as a technique), the meat proxy and babysitting (orchestration, though practices here handle both).

disciplines.name: Harness engineering
disciplines.question: What have you built around your agent: the tools it uses, what it may do on its own, and what each run starts inside?
disciplines.scope_note: Everything around the agent except the model and what it reads. That covers what the agent may reach, the boundary it runs inside, which steps wait for a person, the checks that hold whatever it was told, the plugins, MCP servers and dependencies let in, and the tools made for it. The field calls the whole the agent harness ('Agent = Model + Harness', LangChain). 'Harness engineering' names the discipline, not a practice. In Hashimoto's sense (engineer a fix after every mistake) it is the context discipline's 'a correction sticks'. These live elsewhere: what the agent knows (context); how work is handed over (prompt); whether the work is right, meaning tests, linters, reviewers and evals (verification: the 'sensors' half of guides-and-sensors is backpressure there); agents that run without you, and watching them (orchestration). Hooks, permission settings, sandboxes, plugins and MCP servers are techniques, never practices. The floor is using an agent on real work most days, including tools others connected (v13 harness-1 and harness-4; ruling 7: 'Using them is a L1 basic thing'). It is not a practice. Building something that changes how the agent runs is the L4 level of each practice here, not a practice of its own: v13's build leg (harness-10) is spread across the practices its builds serve. Approval fatigue comes from the vocabulary's 'human' family and lives here because its fixes do. YOLO mode is filed as a move in the vocabulary. Here it is the challenge 'running with every guard off'.

disciplines.name: Orchestration
disciplines.question: How many agents do you run at once, how do their runs start, and how do you keep watch without sitting on them?
disciplines.scope_note: In: work spread over more than one agent (parallel sessions, one job split across agents), agents that run without the person (on a schedule, on an event, looping over a list), how the person keeps an eye on them, what they pass on to others, and what the runs cost. Out: sending exploration to a sub-agent to keep one session clean (context: sub-agent architectures), checks the agent can't talk its way past (verification: backpressure), permission prompts, sandboxing and approving each step (harness: approval fatigue, human-in-the-loop), and agreeing the plan before the work (prompt). Three challenges from the vocabulary's 'human' family live here (babysitting the agent, meat proxy, token maxxing) because their fixes are about where the person's attention goes.

starts-from-zero.name: A new session doesn't know yesterday's work
starts-from-zero.what_goes_wrong: A fresh session knows nothing of yesterday's decisions, dead ends and progress, or the project facts it was already told. The person explains it all again, pastes a summary back in, or the agent guesses.
starts-from-zero.ask: You open a new session on yesterday's task. What does the agent already know before you type anything, and how?
call_signs: Explains the background again at the start of each session
Pastes a summary from the old session
Names notes that the new session reads on its own
Copies answers or context from one AI tool into another
laptop_signs: New sessions whose agent starts by reading notes an earlier session wrote, without being told to
First messages that reach back to earlier work or name an earlier session
Sessions in each project that write into a notes folder

pitfall.title: I fix the same thing by hand in every session and never write it down
pitfall.fix: The second time you correct something, put it where every new session reads it: one line in the project's instructions, with the reason. If the code itself keeps teaching the agent the wrong habit, fix the code instead of adding a rule.
pitfall.why: A fresh session knows nothing of yesterday's decisions, dead ends and progress, or of the project's own facts and the corrections you already made. You explain it all again, or the agent guesses.

pitfall.title: Each AI tool has its own instructions, so I copy-paste between them
pitfall.fix: Keep one shared instruction layer every tool reads (for example AGENTS.md, with each tool's own file pointing to it), so switching tools doesn't mean explaining the project again.
pitfall.why: Another AI tool keeps its own instructions, so you explain the project again or copy results from one tool into the next, and each tool works from a different, partial picture.
pitfall.glance: Context is copied by hand from one tool to the next

pitfall.title: Everyone on the team sets up the agent alone
pitfall.fix: Commit the shared setup (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, shared settings, shared skills) and keep only personal preferences in local files, so every teammate's agent starts from the same ground.
pitfall.why: Each engineer sets the agent up alone. Good rules and fixes never reach teammates, the same mistakes get corrected in parallel, and a new teammate's agent starts from nothing.
pitfall.glance: Fixes never reach teammates, and a new teammate starts from nothing

starts-from-zero.seen_in: Calls: re-explaining the project or pasting old history at the start of every session, nearly always 'no time' to write it down (common-pitfalls rank 3); laptops: first messages that name a file or reach back to an earlier session.

corrections-dont-stick.name: The agent repeats a mistake you already corrected
corrections-dont-stick.what_goes_wrong: The person corrects the agent, it says 'you're right', and the same mistake comes back later in the session or in the next one, because the correction lived only in that chat.
corrections-dont-stick.ask: What was the last correction you gave the agent twice, and what happened after the second time? When did you last delete a line from your rules, and why?
corrections-dont-stick.seen_in: Calls: the same correction typed in every session (pitfalls rank 3); one of his three L3 questions, 'what happens when a correction occurs in-chat?' (substrate-issues/levels.md).

prompt-bloat.name: The instructions that load every time grow until parts get ignored
prompt-bloat.what_goes_wrong: The always-loaded file is generated in one go or gets a new line after every mistake, and nothing is merged or removed. It fills with things the agent could work out from the repo, rules repeat or contradict each other, and the agent ignores the ones that matter. Always-on tools add to the weight.
prompt-bloat.ask: What does the agent read before it starts, and when did you last remove something from it?

pitfall.title: I let the AI write my CLAUDE.md and keep adding rules to it
pitfall.fix: Treat the file as setup work for the codebase: time up front (15 minutes or an hour) writing down how this project is worked on, then let it grow only from real corrections. One line per thing the agent can't work out from the repo, with a reference to more. When a rule is ignored, look for the cause (too long, contradicted, the code teaches the opposite) before adding another, and delete lines whose cause is fixed.

prompt-bloat.seen_in: Calls: generated, README-shaped instruction files in 8+ calls, files of roughly 300 to 600 lines, 'it ignores half of it' (pitfalls rank 4); laptops: instruction files over 200 lines and files that only grow in git.

knowledge-doesnt-reach-the-agent.name: The agent misses the rule or doc that applies here, unless you hand it over
knowledge-doesnt-reach-the-agent.what_goes_wrong: The rule for this module, the deploy steps or the right spec exist, but nothing tells the agent when to read them. So the person pastes paths and docs into every ask, or everything loads everywhere and rules meant for one place leak into another.
knowledge-doesnt-reach-the-agent.ask: Show me where a rule that applies to only one module lives, and how the agent knows to read it there and only there.
knowledge-doesnt-reach-the-agent.seen_in: Calls: specs and decision logs that no line points to, 'our biggest time drain is manually assembling context' (pitfalls rank 10); his L3 question 'how do agents discover instructions and rules, unprompted?'; laptops: prompts that name files.

notes-pile-up.name: Notes, specs and memory files pile up and go stale
notes-pile-up.what_goes_wrong: Notes, decision logs and memory files are added one at a time and never merged or retired. With no overview on top, the agent wades through all of them, misses the one that matters, or follows one that is out of date as if it were current.
notes-pile-up.ask: How big is your notes or memory folder now, and when did you last merge or delete something in it?
call_signs: 'The memory folder just keeps growing': decision logs or notes that are added to and never pruned
The agent used an out-of-date note or doc as if it were current
Keeps a short overview on top that says which note to read for what, and retires settled entries
The notes file is rewritten from scratch every session
Adds to the notes in small edits instead of rewriting them
laptop_signs: Notes or memory files added compared with merged or removed in the last 30 days
Whether an overview or index file exists and is read before the other notes

pitfall.title: My notes and memory only grow: more files, longer lists, nothing merged
pitfall.fix: Consolidate on a rhythm: merge overlapping notes, delete what is settled or wrong, and keep a short overview on top (an index the agent reads first that says which file to read for what), so it never has to wade through every file. Merge with small edits; rewriting the whole store into one summary loses the detail.
pitfall.why: Notes, decision logs, specs and memory files are added one at a time and kept for good. They turn into long lists of small files with no overview on top, so the agent wades through all of them, misses the one that matters, or follows an entry that is out of date.

notes-pile-up.seen_in: Calls: memory folders and decision logs that only grow, a docs gate that read unmerged work as settled fact (pitfalls rank 10).

context-rot.name: A long session gets worse the longer it runs
context-rot.what_goes_wrong: As one session runs for hours or days, the agent forgets the goal and earlier decisions, repeats itself, follows its rules less, and keeps building on a wrong turn that is still in the history. Each automatic compaction loses a little more.

pitfall.title: When it goes wrong, I push harder in the same session
pitfall.fix: After the second miss, stop. Fork the session and, in the side session, ask the agent which instruction or earlier text led it there; fix that. Then go back to before the wrong turn, or start fresh with the corrected fact written first. Say what to do and why, not what not to do.

context-rot.seen_in: Calls: one chat kept for days or weeks on automatic compaction, hallucinations after repeated compactions, 'the AI forgets what is the main purpose' (pitfalls rank 6); correcting a wrong turn in place two or three times (rank 9).

session-fills-with-noise.name: Side questions, dead ends and long output fill the session
session-fills-with-noise.what_goes_wrong: Unrelated questions go into the working session, and big file reads, logs and test runs land in it whole. The session fills with material that has nothing to do with the task, and the work drags.
session-fills-with-noise.ask: When a session is full of dead ends from things you tried, what do you do before you carry on?
call_signs: 'The context is full of failed attempts'
Saves what worked and starts clean
Sends the trial and error to a side session or a sub-agent
One session a day for everything
One session per scope, with side questions in a side session or a sub-agent
'It keeps doing the same kind of step it did earlier'
Starts a fresh session for each new phase of the work
Keeps big tool output out of the session
laptop_signs: Compactions and fresh sessions
Sub-agents' share of the reading
Forks and side sessions opened from a working session
Sub-agents started for side questions
Session length and fullness, compactions, and fresh sessions in the same folder. These are read for context rot and not separated from it today.

pitfall.title: I keep unrelated work in one session and lean on auto-compaction
pitfall.fix: Keep one session per scope. Related tasks that need the same background can share a session; work that needs different background gets its own. When something must carry over, hand it off: a written handoff the next session reads, a hand-off to another agent, or a snapshot into memory the next session loads. Compact only inside one scope, say what must survive, and check the summary.

session-fills-with-noise.seen_in: Calls: 'analyze the whole project' asked in the main session, one session a day for everything (pitfalls practice card 5); laptops: share of file reading done in the main session versus sub-agents.

setup-stays-on-one-laptop.name: What one agent was taught never reaches teammates or other tools
setup-stays-on-one-laptop.what_goes_wrong: Each engineer sets the agent up alone and keeps the files local. Good rules never reach teammates, the same mistakes get corrected in parallel, a new teammate's agent starts from nothing, and each AI tool has its own instructions so context is copied between them by hand.
setup-stays-on-one-laptop.ask: If a new teammate cloned the repo and opened the agent today, what would it know, and whose agent besides yours reads your rules?
setup-stays-on-one-laptop.seen_in: Calls: about 9 people configure agents alone with no shared repo setup (common-pitfalls review, 'not shortlisted but supported'); copying between AI tools (v15 pitfall order 12).

real-context-size.name: The part of the window that works is smaller than the advertised window
real-context-size.term: real context size (claimed versus effective context length)
real-context-size.what_goes_wrong: A model keeps its quality only up to some length, often far below the context size it claims. Filling the advertised window means working past the point where it holds up. The linked practices come from its sibling, the dumb zone: keep use low. Its own source names only evals.
real-context-size.ask: How full do you let a session get before you act, and how did you settle on that point?
call_signs: Names a point well below the full window where they act
Assumes the whole window is safe because it is advertised
laptop_signs: How full the session was when they compacted or started fresh (median)
Whether stepping in rises as sessions fill up

wish-not-task.name: The ask is a wish, so the agent guesses
wish-not-task.what_goes_wrong: The ask says what they want but not where it lives, what finished looks like or what to leave alone. The agent picks its own place to work and its own finish line, and they find out what it decided only by reading the result.
wish-not-task.ask: Read me the last thing you handed the agent, word for word. How did it know where to work and when it was finished?
wish-not-task.seen_in: Calls: naming one ticket fired 15/36, naming the exact file 8/36; the L1 answer is the wish, then 'how do I check all 800 changes?'.

does-more-than-asked.name: The agent does more than was asked
does-more-than-asked.what_goes_wrong: The agent adds files, abstractions, options, tests or docs nobody asked for. The change gets bigger and harder to check than the task needed.
does-more-than-asked.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent did more than you asked: what did it add, and what did you do?
call_signs: 'It made like 800 file changes.'
'It added tests, docs and a config option nobody asked for.'
L2: 'I tell it: only this, and list anything else you'd change at the end.'
laptop_signs: Hand read on the one laptop (goal_drift.py): 8 of 38 early step-ins were the agent going off what was asked or agreed, and 2 of 14 step-ins after a 'done' reply were it taking on more than asked.
Not measured: files the agent changed that the ask never named.
does-more-than-asked.seen_in: Calls: scope limits such as 'don't touch types.ts, other modules depend on it' fired 7/36.

wanders-off.name: The agent drifts away from what was asked
wanders-off.what_goes_wrong: As the run goes on, the agent solves a nearby problem, rewrites more than the one part, or stops at something that only looks finished.
wanders-off.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent ended up somewhere other than where you meant it to go: what had you told it at the start, and when did you notice?
call_signs: 'It rewrote the whole handler when I wanted one branch.'
L1: 'I drop the ticket title in and let it fill in the rest.'
L1: 'It writes a plan file at the end that reads like a changelog, not something I agreed to first.'
L2: 'I stop it the moment it heads somewhere we didn't agree, and say why.'
laptop_signs: Stepping in early in a session (goal_drift.py): Esc while it works, a tool call they rejected, or a message that opens like a correction. On the one laptop read, that was 7.9% of messages 2 to 10. In a hand read of 38, 17 were the agent going off the ask or misreading it, and 19 were the person changing the ask or a message that wasn't theirs.

Whether 'done' was set before the session got going (goal_drift.py): a goal or plan command, plan mode, a long first message, or a plan or spec file named. On that laptop 86 of 445 sessions did this, with no fewer step-ins (4.5% against 4.9%).
Not countable yet: the agent claiming done when it wasn't (0 of 14 hand-read step-ins after a 'done' reply were that).

pitfall.title: I ask for too much at once
pitfall.fix: One change at a time: say where it lives, what done looks like and what to leave alone, and ask it to list extras at the end instead of doing them. Cut the work into steps you can read and commit each. When stages hand over, write each stage's output to a file the next one reads.
pitfall.why: As a run goes on, the agent moves away from what was asked. It solves a nearby problem, rewrites more than the one part, or stops at something that only looks finished.

wanders-off.seen_in: Laptop read: about half of the early step-ins that looked like drift were the person changing the ask, not the agent drifting.

told-not-shown.name: The agent works from their summary instead of the real thing
told-not-shown.what_goes_wrong: They describe the error or the behaviour in their own words instead of handing over the error, the log, the output or the exact fields. The agent fixes what the summary says, which is not always what is broken.
told-not-shown.ask: Read me the last thing you handed the agent, word for word. How did it know where to work and when it was finished?
told-not-shown.seen_in: Calls: asks in exact technical terms (the model, its fields, the real error) fired 7/36.

wrong-design-found-late.name: On a bigger change, the disagreement shows up in the code
wrong-design-found-late.what_goes_wrong: A bigger change starts without an agreed approach. The agent picks a design they would have rejected, and they find out only in the diff, after the work is done.
wrong-design-found-late.ask: Show me a plan or spec from a recent bigger change. Where did you disagree with it, and what did you change before code was written?
wrong-design-found-late.seen_in: Calls: asking for a plan before code fired 15/36 (the strongest prompt cue against the survey); a written spec before starting 10/36.

louder-not-clearer.name: A miss gets repeated louder instead of fixed
louder-not-clearer.what_goes_wrong: When the result is wrong they regenerate, repeat the same instruction in capitals, add another 'don't', or quietly fix it by hand. Nothing in the ask changes, so the same miss comes back.

'By the tenth file it did all of them the same way, even the ones that differ.'

Not measured: the same instruction typed again with more capitals or more 'must'.
Not measured: capitals and must/never in their typed asks, and in the instruction files and skills they wrote. The files are on disk, but today the scan reads their size, not their wording.
Not measured.
louder-not-clearer.seen_in: Calls: naming the defect when sending it back fired 12/36, blaming their own wording only 4/36; the L1 answer is 'it hallucinated' or 'I hit regenerate'.

patched-prompts.name: Reused prompts collect patches until each fix breaks something else
patched-prompts.what_goes_wrong: A prompt they keep and reuse gets one more line after every miss. It grows long and fragile, and a fix for one case starts breaking another.
patched-prompts.ask: Tell me about a prompt or instruction you reuse that has grown through quick fixes: when did you last rewrite it instead of adding to it?
call_signs: 'Every time it breaks I add another line to the prompt.'
'Nobody wants to touch that one; it's a wall of special cases.'
L3: 'Last month I rewrote it from scratch and cut half of it.'
'I fixed that and then it started doing the other thing.'
'I keep patching the prompt and it never gets better.'
L4: 'Before I change it, I rerun the cases that broke before.'
laptop_signs: Size and trim history of their own always-loaded instruction files, read from git (prompt_bloat.py; the context discipline owns that reading).
Not measured: growth, trims and rewrites of the skills, commands and sub-agent instructions they wrote. The files are on disk and in git, but no check reads their history.
Not measured. It could be read as an edit to one of their kept prompts followed, in later sessions, by corrections about a different behaviour.
Evals they wrote are seen (no_backpressure.py), but not tied to the prompt they test.
patched-prompts.seen_in: Calls: reusing prompts from a kept folder fired 4/36; the playbook itself teaches 'add a rule after every correction' (v15 open question).

agrees-with-your-guess.name: The agent agrees with the guess in the question
agrees-with-your-guess.what_goes_wrong: They put their own guess about the cause into the ask. The agent confirms it instead of looking elsewhere, and flips its answer the moment they push back.
agrees-with-your-guess.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent agreed with you and you turned out to be wrong: how did you find out?
call_signs: 'It said I was absolutely right and changed it back.'
'It agrees with whatever I suggest.'
L2: 'I don't tell it which option I like, and I ask for the case against.'
'I told it I thought it was the cache and it spent an hour in the cache.'
L2: 'I give it the symptom and ask for a few possible causes before I say mine.'
laptop_signs: Not measured. The logs carry the agent's replies, so a few things could be counted: an agreeing reply right after the person pushes back, followed by the agent undoing its own work.
Not measured.
agrees-with-your-guess.seen_in: Calls: the L1 answer is 'it agreed with me, so I went with it'; the L2 answer is 'be critical, push back, we need hard evidence'.

prompt-overfitting.name: A prompt tuned on a few cases fails on the next one
prompt-overfitting.what_goes_wrong: A reused prompt, or its examples, gets tuned on the few cases someone tried. It does well on those and worse on new ones. This mostly bites people who keep prompts (skills, sub-agent instructions) and reuse them on new work.
prompt-overfitting.ask: Tell me about the last time a prompt you reuse worked on the cases you tried and then failed on a new one: what had you tried it on?
call_signs: 'It worked on my three examples and fell over on the client's data.'
L4: 'I keep some cases aside that I never tune on.'
laptop_signs: Not measured.

false-done.name: The agent says it's done when it isn't
false-done.what_goes_wrong: The agent reports done, or 'all tests pass', without running anything end to end, testing the wrong layer, or leaving parts out (stubs, placeholders, skipped steps). The person finds the gap later.
false-done.ask: The agent says it's done and everything passes. Tell me about the last time that wasn't true: how did you find out?
call_signs: 'It said done and it wasn't': nothing had been run, the wrong layer was tested, or a step was skipped
Takes the summary's word, or asks the same session 'does this look good?' (the level guide's L1 line)
Found stubs, placeholders or skipped parts after the agent said it had finished
Has to ask again for the parts it left out

Code commits with nothing run after the agent's last edit (comprehension_debt.py)

Not read today: placeholders or 'to do' notes added in the agent's last edits. The closest reading: a finish check they built refusing because parts were missing (no_backpressure.py).

gamed-checks.name: The agent makes the check pass instead of fixing the problem
gamed-checks.what_goes_wrong: The agent gets to green by deleting or skipping the failing test, weakening what it checks, faking the thing under test, or writing code that only works for the test's inputs. The report says everything passes and the problem is still there.
gamed-checks.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent got a check to pass without really fixing the problem. How did you find out?
call_signs: Heard on a call: 'if you're auto approving stuff, you end up removing test because they are not working. And it's probably because something is actually broken.'
Tells of a test the agent deleted, skipped or rewrote to go green
Found out only later, when the bug came back in real use
A fix that passed the tests and then failed on the first real input
Mentions hard-coded values, or a branch that only exists for the test

A test file edited in the same session just before the first passing run (not read separately today)

pitfall.title: I believe 'done, all tests pass' from the agent that wrote the code
pitfall.fix: Before it starts, say what outcome proves the work: an end-to-end run, a migration that succeeds on a local copy, a preview you can click through. Ask the agent for that outcome and its proof (the command and its real output), not a story of its steps. Don't let the agent change the test to make it pass, and tell it to report a wrong test instead of changing it.

agents-word-wins.name: The agent that wrote the work is the one that says it's fine
agents-word-wins.what_goes_wrong: The person asks the same chat 'does this look good?', or treats a confident summary or a green tick as the proof. An agent checking its own work praises it, and its word wins over the person's own doubt.
agents-word-wins.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent's answer and your own sense of the code disagreed. Which one won, and how did it turn out?
call_signs: Went with the agent's answer against their own doubt, and it turned out wrong
Treats 'tests pass' or the agent's summary as the proof
laptop_signs: Not separated today. It reads the same as comprehension debt: commits with nothing checked after the last edit.
Tool calls the person rejected would show the opposite. They are in the logs but not read yet.
agents-word-wins.seen_in: The level guide's L1 line for l2-s-08 ('ask the same chat does this look good'); a separate reviewer was v13's strongest verification signal (24/92 calls).

shipped-unread.name: Work ships that nobody read or can explain
shipped-unread.what_goes_wrong: It works when clicked once, so it goes out. Underneath it touched files it shouldn't have or fixed the symptom, and the person can't walk through it. Teammates or the client end up doing the review, and every later change costs more.
shipped-unread.ask: Tell me about the last change the agent wrote that went out. How did you know it was right?
call_signs: Can't walk through one function of a change they shipped

Opens pull requests straight from the agent without reading them first
Says some kinds of agent output go in unread (small fixes, config, copy). v13 counted this against them.
Pastes errors back to the agent without looking at the code
Can't say what they thought before asking the agent
The reason for a design choice is 'the agent suggested it'
Avoids working without the agent, or struggles to, even on small things
Can't take over a problem the agent couldn't solve

pitfall.title: The agent writes faster than I can review, so I skim and ship
pitfall.fix: Your attention is the bottleneck, so spend it on outcomes, not on every step. Decide up front what proves the change (a dry run on a local copy, a preview branch you see running, the result of a spike) and ask the agent to report those outcomes. Read line by line only where a mistake is costly: auth, money, data. Never pass on work you can't explain.

shipped-unread.seen_in: 11/92 calls say some agent output goes in unread; l2-s-07's L1 line: 'I check if the results make sense, then commit'.

same-miss-again.name: The same kind of defect comes back
same-miss-again.what_goes_wrong: A defect in the agent's work gets caught and fixed by hand, but nothing would catch it next time, so the same kind of mistake ships again in a later session or a teammate's.
same-miss-again.ask: Tell me about a bug the agent made that you caught. What makes sure that one can't come back?
same-miss-again.seen_in: 51/92 calls name a specific defect the agent made; few say what stops it coming back (v13 Failure capture).

setup-change-untested.name: A change to the agent's instructions makes things worse and nobody notices
setup-change-untested.what_goes_wrong: The person edits a prompt, a rule file or a reviewer they set up, tries it once, and calls it fine. A case that used to work breaks and nobody finds out until it bites.
setup-change-untested.ask: When you last changed a prompt, rule or helper agent, how did you know it didn't get worse? Name a case and what it checks.
setup-change-untested.seen_in: On laptops, hundreds of edits to instruction files against a handful of eval runs; on calls evals are mostly a plan (a member call, 10-13).

doom-loop.name: The agent keeps trying the same failing fix
doom-loop.what_goes_wrong: The agent goes round in circles on a problem it can't solve. It tries one blind fix after another, often without running the code in between, or repeats the same error across sessions. The vocabulary's other fixes (starting clean, saving the correction where the next session reads it) belong to context.
doom-loop.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent got stuck fixing something. What did you do?
call_signs: 'It kept going in circles', and nothing about the approach changed
Gave up on the task, or kept pasting the same error back
Describes breaking the loop: stopped it, named the real cause, changed the approach, or started clean
laptop_signs: The same check failing 3+ times in a row with the same error, and edits aimed at that error (doom_loop.py). One laptop had none in 30 days: all 40 runs of 3+ failures were normal fix-and-retest, and a hand check of 13 held that up.
Who broke each loop (the person stepping in, a reset, or the agent alone) and whether it ended in a passing run

tools-made-for-people.name: The agent fumbles tools made for people
tools-made-for-people.what_goes_wrong: The agent works through commands and services built for a person at a screen. It scrolls through pages of output, guesses options and misreads errors, so turns and attention go to the tool instead of the task.
tools-made-for-people.ask: Tell me about the last time the agent got stuck on a command or a service, like too much output, a wrong option or something it couldn't reach. What did you change?
call_signs: Copies tickets, logs or database rows in by hand because the agent can't reach them
Uses connections others set up: the floor, a Level 1 basic (ruling 7), not evidence of the practice
Wrote a script or command whose output is shaped for the agent, or built a tool server with commands they designed
laptop_signs: Connected services called per server and outside tools run from the shell (using them is the floor)
Tool servers they wrote: no check yet (scan coverage, table 5)
tools-made-for-people.seen_in: Calls: 'it got stuck on the command' stories; the field names only the fix (agent-computer interface), not the problem.

cant-reach-the-system.name: The agent can't reach the system, so they paste it in
cant-reach-the-system.what_goes_wrong: The build log, the ticket, the error report or the database rows live where the agent can't get to them. The engineer copies them in by hand, every time, and the agent works from whatever slice they happened to paste.
cant-reach-the-system.ask: Tell me about the last time you pasted something into the agent, a log, a ticket, a query result, or watched it get stuck on a command. Could it have fetched that itself, and what did you change?
cant-reach-the-system.seen_in: v13 calls: 44 of 110 name a system outside the code the agent reaches, 35 of 110 a connection; the rest describe pasting.

rule-in-words-ignored.name: A rule written in the instructions gets broken anyway
rule-in-words-ignored.what_goes_wrong: A rule that must hold every time (never commit a secrets file, never force-push, format what you write) is only written in the instructions. Most of the time the agent follows it; sometimes it doesn't, and the engineer finds out after, then adds the rule again in louder words.
rule-in-words-ignored.ask: Which rule does your agent have to follow every single time, and what happens when it doesn't? What stops it, and when did that last fire?
rule-in-words-ignored.seen_in: Pitfall cards 4 and 9 (19 and more people in calls): a new line in the instructions after every mistake, repeated louder.

approval-fatigue.name: Every action asks for approval, so 'yes' becomes a reflex
approval-fatigue.what_goes_wrong: The agent asks so often that the engineer clicks yes without reading. The one request that mattered goes through like the rest, and the waiting pushes them to switch the questions off altogether.
approval-fatigue.ask: How often does the agent stop to ask your permission, and when did you last say no?
call_signs: Can tell the last time they said no and why
'I just click yes', or clicks through to keep moving
Prompts come up only on the risky steps because routine ones are allowed in their settings
laptop_signs: Permission mode on each typed message: all checks off, automatic, plan, ask
Allow, ask and refuse rule counts and the default mode in settings
Minutes agents wait on the person (waiting check: one laptop, about 3 minutes per agent hour, half of it plan approvals)
In the logs but not read yet: tool calls the person rejected (157 in 14 days on one laptop), the plainest sign prompts are read
Permission prompts themselves leave no record

yolo-mode.name: Every permission prompt is switched off
yolo-mode.what_goes_wrong: To stop the waiting, everything is approved by default on their own machine, with their keys, client code, production access and network in reach. Nothing stands between a wrong guess and lasting damage: a dropped table, a push to the main branch, a secret sent out.
yolo-mode.ask: When the agent runs without asking you anything, what's the worst it could do on that machine, and what would stop it?
call_signs: Auto-approves everything to go faster on their own machine (level guide: the Level 1 line of 'What the agent doesn't get to do')
Runs without prompts only inside a container, a virtual machine or a throwaway copy
Keeps refuse rules or guards that still hold with prompts off (refuse rules block in every mode, per the permission docs)
Names something the agent can't reach and the mechanism they set up that enforces it (was v13 hn-perm-scoped)
laptop_signs: Share of typed messages run with all permission checks off (one laptop: 95%)
Settings that skip the warning for the all-off mode
Whether a boundary was in use: sandbox switched on in settings, repos with a dev container. Commands marked as sandboxed are in the logs but not read yet
Refuse rules and guards that can block, wired in settings
Refuse rules in settings, the sandbox switched on, repos with a dev container
Secrets lying in plain files the agent can open: no check yet

pitfall.title: The agent can reach production or secrets, and I approve everything to keep it moving
pitfall.fix: Decide per project how much the agent may reach: there is no one rule. Inside a sandbox with no production access, skipping prompts can be fine. Outside one, give it only the access the task needs, keep secrets and production out of its reach, and make sure there is a way back (a branch, a backup) before anything that can't be undone.
pitfall.why: To stop the prompts, everything gets approved, on a machine with your keys, client code and network in reach. Nothing stands between a wrong guess or an injected instruction and the damage. The agent's own docs say running without prompts is for isolated containers and virtual machines only.

yolo-mode.seen_in: Pitfall card 7: checks off on a laptop holding client code and keys; one laptop ran 95% of typed messages with every check off.

lethal-trifecta.name: Private data, text from outside and a way out are in one session
lethal-trifecta.what_goes_wrong: The agent holds private data (a client database, a secrets file), reads text anyone could have written (a web page, an email, an issue) and can send things out (a message, a push, an upload). An instruction hidden in that text can make it send the data out. Any one or two of the three is far safer than all three in one session, and a send that stops for a person, or a hook that blocks it, takes the third away.
lethal-trifecta.ask: In one session, can the agent read your private data, read text from outside, and send something out? Which of the three could you take away, and what would it cost you?
call_signs: Names systems outside the code the agent reaches, like the database, the deploy platform, the error tracker or team chat (was v13 hn-service-wired). This is exposure, not skill
Removes one of the three on purpose: no outside network while it reads client data, or no secrets on the machine it runs on
Sends and pushes that stop for a person, or a hook that blocks the ones that would leak
laptop_signs: Connected services the agent called and outside tools it ran from the shell (private data and ways out)
Web fetches in the same sessions (untrusted text)
Ask rules, refuse rules and hooks that can block, over the ways out (a send, a push, an upload, a deploy)
lethal-trifecta.seen_in: A tester with private data debugging in the same sessions as web reading and Slack, git and Drive sends: all the ways out sat behind her ask rules and a commit-blocking hook, so it did not show.

each-run-set-up-by-hand.name: Every run is set up by hand
each-run-set-up-by-hand.what_goes_wrong: Each run starts from nothing: open a session, pick the branch or copy, paste the same opening setup, start the helpers one by one. Steps get skipped, two runs of the same job start differently, and a teammate can't start it the same way at all.
each-run-set-up-by-hand.ask: Walk me through how a run starts, from nothing to the agent working. Which of those steps did you build, and how do you know it still works after you change it?
each-run-set-up-by-hand.seen_in: v13 build-leg probe (35 calls): 9 wrote their own agent roles, 3 their own program that starts the agent; the rest start every run by typing.

babysitting.name: You watch the agent work instead of working
babysitting.what_goes_wrong: You sit with the agent while it runs: approving each step, typing 'continue', correcting it as it goes. It can only move as fast as your attention, and you get nothing else done meanwhile.
babysitting.ask: Tell me about the last long task you gave an agent: what were you doing while it worked, and what made you go back to it?
call_signs: Says they sit and watch the agent work, or can't leave it alone
Approves each step, or keeps typing 'continue' to move it on
Describes most of their day as supervising and correcting agents rather than building
laptop_signs: Minutes the agents sat waiting for them per agent hour: questions, plan approvals, turns that ended on a question (about 3 on one laptop)
Long runs they stayed to watch: replied within a minute with nothing typed in any other session (16 of 507 long runs on one laptop)
Esc interrupts, rejected tool calls and messages typed while the agent was still busy
Short go-ahead replies ('yes', 'continue') that keep a run moving
babysitting.seen_in: Calls: 'I sit and watch it', 'continue' to keep it moving; one laptop: about 3 minutes of agent waiting per agent hour, 16 of 507 long runs watched.

unwatched-run-goes-wrong.name: A run left alone goes wrong and nobody notices
unwatched-run-goes-wrong.what_goes_wrong: You stop watching and the run loops, stalls, runs for hours or wanders off the task. You find out when you come back, after the time and money are spent, so you stop trusting runs enough to leave them.
unwatched-run-goes-wrong.ask: Tell me about the last long task you gave an agent: what did you tell it done meant, what were you doing while it worked, and what brought you back to it?
unwatched-run-goes-wrong.seen_in: v13 call: '20 agents working at the same time' followed by 'I cannot just let them go'.

one-at-a-time.name: Your attention sets the pace: one agent at a time, and you wait
one-at-a-time.what_goes_wrong: Only one thing runs with the agent, and you wait for each answer before starting the next. Your own reading of what comes back is what limits how much gets done, and the work is not sized to it.
one-at-a-time.ask: What were your agents doing during your last meeting?
call_signs: One session at a time, waiting for each answer before starting the next thing
Nothing else runs while the agent works: they read along, wait, or switch to email
Says parallel work feels unsafe because sessions step on each other's files
Names their own reading of the agent's output as what limits how much gets done
laptop_signs: Share of the agents' busy time with only one agent working (23% with sub-agents counted, on one laptop)
Stretches where they waited on a single agent and came straight back to that session (65 stretches, about 5 hours in 28 days, on one laptop)
Runs that went on while they were away, and whether they ended in kept work
one-at-a-time.seen_in: 16 of 92 v13 calls name their own review as the bottleneck; one laptop: 65 stretches (about 5 hours in 28 days) waiting on a single agent.

agents-share-a-checkout.name: Agents running at once undo each other's changes
agents-share-a-checkout.what_goes_wrong: Several agents work at the same time in one copy of the code. One overwrites or reverts another's changes, a test run picks up another agent's half-finished work, and nobody can tell which agent broke what.
agents-share-a-checkout.ask: When you last had two agents working at once, where did each one's changes live, and did one ever undo the other's?
call_signs: Runs several agents at once in the same folder
Says one agent overwrote or reverted another's changes
Opens each task in its own worktree and knows which session holds which
laptop_signs: Stretches with two or more agents editing at once in the same working directory, compared with ones in separate worktrees

pitfall.title: I run several agents in the same checkout and they step on each other
pitfall.fix: Give each parallel agent its own working copy (a git worktree per ticket), and run no more at once than you can read back. A worktree separates files, not databases or ports, so plan for those too.
pitfall.why: Several agents work at the same time in one copy of the code. One overwrites or reverts another's changes, a test run picks up another agent's half-finished work, and nobody can tell which agent broke what.

meat-proxy.name: More comes back than you can read, so it goes on unread
meat-proxy.grade: emerging (slang with a defining source; widely repeated since 2026-08)
meat-proxy.what_goes_wrong: With several agents running, their output piles up faster than you can read it. Pull requests go to review unread, reviewers' comments go straight back to the agent, and colleagues end up doing the engineering.
meat-proxy.ask: Tell me about the last change an agent wrote that went to a colleague for review: what had you read before you sent it, and how did you answer their comments?
call_signs: Sent a pull request for review that they hadn't read, or can't explain a change they shipped
Pastes reviewers' comments to the agent and forwards its reply
Answers colleagues with what the agent said, in the agent's words

parts-dont-fit.name: One job split across agents comes back in pieces that don't fit
parts-dont-fit.what_goes_wrong: Several agents take parts of the same job with nobody saying who owns which part or what each must hand back. Two do the same work, one changes what another relies on, and the time saved goes into stitching the results together.
parts-dont-fit.ask: Tell me about one job you split across several agents: who did which part, what did each hand back, and how did you put it together and check it?

work-stops-when-you-stop.name: Agent work happens only while you are typing
work-stops-when-you-stop.what_goes_wrong: Every run starts because you typed it. Routine jobs (triage a new ticket, check the nightly build, answer a failing pipeline) wait until you are at the keyboard, so nothing moves while you are in a meeting, asleep or on other work.
work-stops-when-you-stop.ask: Tell me about the last time an agent went through a long list of items: where was it kept what was done, and what happened when a run failed or stopped halfway?
work-stops-when-you-stop.seen_in: v13: 7 members with runs started by a ticket, webhook or schedule against most calls where every run is typed; one laptop: no OS job starts an agent.

long-job-loses-its-place.name: A long job in one session loses its place
long-job-loses-its-place.what_goes_wrong: A long list of work (every file, every ticket, a backlog) runs in one session. It gets worse as the session fills, and when it crashes or you stop it the progress is gone and you restart it by hand.
long-job-loses-its-place.ask: Tell me about the last time an agent went through a long list of items: where was it kept what was done, and what happened when a run failed or stopped halfway?
long-job-loses-its-place.seen_in: v13: 4 members had a system walk a whole set on its own, 2 had runs carry on past a failure; resuming was never asked, so it read 0.

token-maxxing.name: Agent runs cost more than what they leave
token-maxxing.grade: standard (as workplace slang: Wikipedia, WSJ, Forbes, Business Insider, Axios and The Pragmatic Engineer use it the same way; no coiner)
token-maxxing.what_goes_wrong: Agent use becomes the goal: many agents and long runs, little of it kept, often because usage is watched or ranked. The strongest model does routine work, nothing caps a run nobody watches, and nobody checks what landed.
token-maxxing.ask: Think of the last day you ran a lot of agent work: how much of what it produced did you keep, and how did you know it was worth what it cost?
call_signs: Counts agents or tokens as the achievement ('I had 20 agents running') without saying what landed
Starts agents on work they don't mean to keep, or because usage is being watched
Can't say what a heavy day of agent work left behind

Many agents at once on days with little kept work: agents at once read beside commits per hour of their attention (one_at_a_time.py)
Cost per session (read and summed into one number only; nothing compares it with what was kept)
Why they ran it (a leaderboard, a target) is never on the laptop: ask on the call

pitfall.title: I burn tokens without checking what they bought
pitfall.fix: Look at what consumes tokens (ask a second session to read a run and report waste). Plan with a strong model and run mechanical work on a cheaper one. Give each agent one job and a small context, point it at files rather than letting it explore, tell it to write a script for bulk data instead of reading it. Load only the tools a task needs. Judge a day by what landed, not by tokens burned. Prove the basic loop on one small task before an expensive process.

results-stuck-in-one-session.name: What one session found stays stuck there, and you carry it to the next by hand
results-stuck-in-one-session.what_goes_wrong: Several sessions work on related parts of the same effort at once, but none of them knows what the others found or changed. You copy findings, file names and decisions from one session into another, notice too late that two of them collided, and become the message bus between your own agents.

goal-drift.name: The agent drifts away from what was asked

write-down-what-it-cannot-know.name: Turn a repeated correction into a line every session reads, and keep those lines few
write-down-what-it-cannot-know.what_you_do: When the agent gets a fact wrong that it can't work out from the repo, or the same correction comes a second time, they write one line, with its reason, where every new session reads it. If the code itself keeps teaching the wrong habit, they fix the code instead. They decide what earns a line, cut what the agent does anyway, settle rules that clash, and remove a rule once its cause is fixed, so the always-loaded part stays short.

ladder.L1: They correct the same mistake again in every session, or work from a long generated file nobody reads or trims.
ladder.L2: They retype the fact or correction into the session each time it is needed, and trim the file only when it visibly bites.
ladder.L3: After the second time, the fact or correction is one line in a file every new session loads, the file stays short enough that they can say why each line is there, and an ignored rule sends them looking for the cause, not for louder wording.
ladder.L4: They built their own tooling that turns repeated corrections into proposed rules and flags oversize, duplicate or dead ones with nobody asking, keep tuning it as their projects change, and re-running an old failure in a fresh session checks that each rule still holds.

techniques.how: A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the repo root that every session loads, CLAUDE.local.md for what is only theirs; /memory to edit what loads and /context to see it.
techniques.laptop_signal: Instruction files per repo and their size, and which of them load at the start of a session

techniques.how: After a correction, ask the agent to add the line under a written rule: one line, the reason, no README text. An agent-written file counts only when supervised this way.
Fix the naming or code that keeps misleading the agent instead of writing a rule against it.
Write rules as what to do, with the reason; keep emphasis for a rule that is actually being skipped; delete lines whose cause is fixed.
A review that compares the rules with recent sessions (ignored rules, corrections not yet captured), or a CI check that fails on size limits and repeated rules.

write-down-what-it-cannot-know.call_evidence: What was the last correction you gave the agent twice, and what happened after the second time? When did you last delete a line from your rules, and why?
write-down-what-it-cannot-know.laptop_evidence: Instruction files in the repos they work in, which of them load at the start of a session, who wrote them (git), and edits to them right after a correction in the same session. That last signal is a lead, not proof.
rulings: Ruling 5: 'It does count, if the way it writes CLAUDE.mds is supervised and doesn't just grow into context rot / pollution.'
Level guide: 'Having a CLAUDE.md is not Level 3 on its own. A team's file counts only if they can say what it does and how.'
L2 to L3 border (10-23): who carries the context, them or a setup they engineered.

practice_card.title: Do it once together, then turn the correction into a rule or a skill
practice_card.text: After you steer the agent, ask where the instruction should live so the next session finds it (root file, nested file, skill). After a repeated task that was slow, ask it to turn the process into a skill (add a script if the steps are fixed). When it goes wrong, paste the failed session into a fresh session and ask why it chose that path and what instruction would have prevented it, then fix the file the answer points to. Prune what no longer applies.

write-down-what-it-cannot-know.authors_note: The field names the files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) but not the act. The nearest name is harness engineering in its narrow sense (every time the agent errs, engineer a fix so it never happens again). The substrate already uses that as a discipline name.

ladder_short.L3: Turns a repeated correction into one short line every session loads
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that drafts and prunes the rules

put-rules-where-they-apply.name: Scope each rule to where it applies, and load deeper docs only when the task needs them
put-rules-where-they-apply.what_you_do: They put each rule in the narrowest place that still reaches where it is needed: the client folder, the repo, a module. Deeper docs, specs and repeated procedures sit behind a pointer that names when to open them ('before changing how data is stored, read the decisions folder'), so the agent finds them on its own and the detail loads only when the task calls for it. Only the outside connections a project needs are switched on.

ladder.L1: Everything sits in one file or nowhere, and the agent works without the rule or doc that applies.
ladder.L2: They carry the knowledge in by hand each session: they say which part's rules apply, point at the files, or paste the doc.
ladder.L3: Rules are split by repo or folder and load only there, and pointers name the situation that sends the agent to a deeper doc or a repeated procedure, so it opens them unprompted.
ladder.L4: They built their own delivery that puts the right rule or doc in front of the agent the moment a matching file, command or task comes up, with no pointer to maintain, keep tuning it as the work changes, and a test shows it fires when it should and stays quiet otherwise.

techniques.how: CLAUDE.md files in subfolders and path-scoped rule files under .claude/rules/; a parent-folder file shared by related repos.
A short router file: hard rules plus one-line triggers ('working on X, read Y'). Test it by asking the agent to work on a module and watching which files it opens.
Skills they wrote: the description always loads, the body only when the task matches (ruling 4: L3).
techniques.laptop_signal: Own skills, decided by git

techniques.how: MCP servers connected per project (.mcp.json) instead of globally; tool search keeps definitions out until needed.
techniques.laptop_signal: Outside tool servers configured and used

techniques.how: A hook that adds a rule or doc when a matching file or command comes up.
techniques.laptop_signal: Hooks that add context, and own hooks, decided by git

put-rules-where-they-apply.call_evidence: Show me where a rule that applies to only one module lives, and how the agent knows to read it there and only there.
put-rules-where-they-apply.laptop_evidence: Words loaded at the start of every session compared with words loaded only when needed; subfolder files that reached the agent and in how many sessions; own skills (git); tool servers per project.
rulings: Ruling 4: writing skills is 'L3', part of the Level 3 picture, not a ticket into it.
Ruling 2: 'Setting up claude's behavior via hooks tooling or anything else, is mostly L4.'
v13 precision ruling, kept: opening the agent from one narrow folder decides nothing; what the instruction layer does decides everything.

practice_card.title: A short router CLAUDE.md, with the detail in folders and skills
practice_card.text: The top file holds only what or when, then where: hard rules and one-line triggers like 'working on X, read Y'. Detail sits in nested per-folder files, index files, skills or a parent-folder file shared by related repos (Claude also reads parent folders' CLAUDE.md). Test the routing by asking the agent to work on a module and checking which files it opens.

ladder_short.L3: Splits rules by folder, with pointers saying when to open deeper docs
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that loads each rule as it applies

notes-the-next-chat-reads.name: Keep what the work has learned in notes the next session reads on its own
notes-the-next-chat-reads.what_you_do: They keep decisions, dead ends, progress and the plan in files outside the session, in a shape they chose: an overview plus a few files, a plan file per feature, a dated decisions log. The agent updates them in small edits as it goes, and a fresh session reads them before they type. Settled or wrong notes are merged or retired so the store stays usable. Who types the notes doesn't matter; who decided their shape does.

ladder.L1: Each session starts from nothing, or a built-in memory 'just remembers' and they can't say what it holds.
ladder.L2: They paste a summary into the new session, or tell each new session which notes file to open.
ladder.L3: A fresh session knows yesterday before they type, because their setup sends it to notes in a shape they designed, which the agent keeps current and which they keep pruned.
ladder.L4: They built their own tooling that writes, prunes and loads the notes without them and blocks work from landing until the record is written, keep reshaping it as their work changes, and a check shows the notes stay right instead of drifting.

techniques.how: A notes folder with an index file, and a line in the always-loaded file telling the agent to read the index first.
A plan or progress file per feature that the agent updates as it works and the next session reads.
techniques.laptop_signal: Writes to files named like memory, status, plan or handoff (matched by name)

techniques.how: Auto-memory or a sub-agent memory folder, counted only with a structure they designed and actually read.
A session-start hook that loads the notes; a blocking hook that refuses to finish until the record is written.

notes-the-next-chat-reads.call_evidence: You open a new session on yesterday's task. What does the agent know before you type anything, and how did it get there?
notes-the-next-chat-reads.laptop_evidence: Per project: the share of new sessions that start by reading notes an earlier session wrote without being told, sessions that write into a notes folder, and first messages that reach back to earlier work or name an earlier session (the person carrying it). Memory is matched by folder or file name, so a notes file with another name scores zero.
rulings: 10-19: 'Who writes the notes doesn't matter: what matters is how their setup is structured and the disciplines they keep.'
10-16: 'everybody has some sort of notes that carry over sessions... but it's more about, did they engineer the context?' Built-in features measure the tool, not the person.
Level guide row 8: building memory systems is where Level 4 starts ('the program doesn't teach').
notes-the-next-chat-reads.authors_note: Merges context offloading (the file system as context), structured note-taking (agentic memory), and recitation (a plan or todo file the agent rewrites so the goal stays in view).

ladder_short.L2: Points each new session at the notes, or pastes a summary in
ladder_short.L3: Designs and prunes notes that every new session reads unprompted

notes-the-next-chat-reads.entry_rules: 1: pitfalls rank 6 and 10, members who cope move state into files, laptop check for first messages naming a file; 2: designing the notes' shape is the person's act (ruling 10-19); 3: their own work, not an agent product's memory.

reset-with-a-handoff.name: Keep each session to one scope, and restart it with a handoff when it degrades
reset-with-a-handoff.what_you_do: Related tasks that need the same background share a session; work that needs different background gets its own. They notice when a session has gone bad (it repeats itself, forgets decisions, makes the same mistake again) and start clean, carrying over only the goal, what's done, what worked and what failed. They go back to before a wrong turn instead of correcting on top of it, and if they compact, they do it inside one scope and say what must survive.

ladder.L1: They keep one session going for days on automatic compaction, and push harder in the same session when it goes wrong.
ladder.L2: They spot a bad session and start clean by hand with a handoff, rewind to before a wrong turn, or compact at a point they chose with a list of what to keep.
ladder.L3: Starting clean costs them nothing: their setup writes the handoff in a fixed shape and the next session picks it up unprompted, and standing instructions decide what survives a compaction.
ladder.L4: They built their own automation that resets or compacts a session at a threshold they set and reloads its state from files without them stepping in, keep tuning the threshold and the saved state as their work changes, and a test shows the next session carries on correctly.

techniques.how: /clear then a first message carrying the handoff; /rewind to a checkpoint before the wrong turn; /fork or /branch for a side idea; claude --resume for a still-good session.
/compact with focus instructions ('keep the file list and open decisions'); a status line that shows how full the context is.
A handoff file: goal, progress, what worked, what didn't, next step.
techniques.laptop_signal: First messages that name an earlier session or a handoff file

techniques.how: Their own handoff command or skill; compaction instructions in the always-loaded file.
Hooks before a compaction and at the session start that follows, to save and reload state.

reset-with-a-handoff.call_evidence: How do you know a session has gone bad, and what does the next session start with?
reset-with-a-handoff.laptop_evidence: Clears compared with compactions; correction streaks followed by a fresh session, a clear or a fork rather than carrying on, and whether step-ins dropped afterwards; forks; first messages that hand over an earlier session. Answer quality isn't in the logs, only the person's reaction to it.

isolate-side-work.name: Keep exploration and long output out of the main session
isolate-side-work.grade: standard ('context quarantine' as a label: emerging)
isolate-side-work.what_you_do: When answering one question means reading a lot of code, logs or docs, they send that reading elsewhere, to a sub-agent with a short brief or to a fork of the session, and only the result comes back. Long output, such as a log or a test run, is filtered by a script before the agent reads it. They know a sub-agent starts blank and needs a brief, while a fork already knows everything the session knows.

ladder.L1: Everything happens in the main session: 'analyze the whole project', whole logs, side questions.
ladder.L2: They send the digging to a sub-agent or a branch by hand when it comes up, with a short brief, or start a workflow that spreads the reading over many sub-agents.
ladder.L3: Their setup does it without them asking: sub-agents they defined get the exploration by default, and a standing rule filters big output before it is read.
ladder.L4: They built their own filters and helper agents that keep bulky reading out of the main session without them asking, keep tuning them as their tasks change, and a test shows the main session stays small on a task that used to flood it.

techniques.how: The Agent tool with the built-in Explore sub-agent, or a custom agent in .claude/agents/ with its own tools and model.
techniques.laptop_signal: Sub-agents started (type, model), what each was sent to do, and the sub-agents' share of file reading

techniques.how: /subtask or the fork sub-agent: a branch that knows the session and returns only the result; dynamic workflows over many sub-agents (ruling 11: L2).
Have the agent write a script (grep, jq, a small program) that reads the bulk and prints only what matters.

isolate-side-work.call_evidence: When the agent needs to read a lot of code to answer one question, where does that reading happen, and what comes back?
isolate-side-work.laptop_evidence: Sub-agents started and what they were sent to do, the share of reading done in sub-agents rather than the main session, forks and branch sub-agents, and workflow runs. File reads through shell commands in the main session are not counted as reading yet.
rulings: Ruling 3: sending exploration to a sub-agent is an 'L2 thing that carries over in L3'.
Ruling 11: dynamic workflows are 'an L2 thing'. Building your own orchestration program that starts agents is still Level 4.
Badge validation: sub-agents the agent spawns on its own are not the person's practice (no credit for sub-agents they didn't ask for or define).
isolate-side-work.authors_note: Merges sub-agent architectures (context isolation, context quarantine) and programmatic tool calling (big results are processed in code, outside the session).

ladder_short.L3: Defines sub-agents that take exploration by default, and filters long output
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests filters and sub-agents that keep the session small

share-the-setup-with-the-team.name: Commit the agent's rules and notes to the team repo, for every teammate and tool
share-the-setup-with-the-team.what_you_do: The rules, pointers and notes every agent on the repo needs are committed in the team's repository, kept apart on purpose from what is only theirs. One shared instruction layer is read by every AI tool the team uses. Teammates' agents run on the same files and teammates add to them, so a new teammate who clones the repo has a productive first session.

ladder.L1: Their setup lives only on their laptop and in one tool, and each teammate starts from nothing.
ladder.L2: They pass tips and rules to teammates by hand, in a message or a session, and copy context between tools.
ladder.L3: The shared setup is committed in the team repo with personal parts kept apart, one layer serves every tool, and named teammates' agents use it and some teammates edit it.
ladder.L4: They built their own tooling that delivers the shared setup to every teammate's agent without anyone stepping in, keep refining it as the team and repo change, and a check on a fresh clone shows a new teammate's agent starts with it.

techniques.how: A committed AGENTS.md as the one file every tool reads, with CLAUDE.md and other tools' rule files pointing to it; CLAUDE.local.md (kept out of git) for what is personal.
Project settings and .mcp.json committed so every developer gets the same connections.
A team plugin with shared skills, agents and hooks, installed by everyone.
techniques.laptop_signal: Own plugins (what they change is not read)

share-the-setup-with-the-team.call_evidence: If a new teammate cloned the repo and opened the agent today, what would it know, and whose agent besides yours reads your rules?
share-the-setup-with-the-team.laptop_evidence: Instruction files committed per repo, and how many authors edited them (git). Whether teammates' agents actually load them happens on their machines and can't be seen here.
rulings: Ruling 2: 'Setting up context either for themselves or the team is L3. Setting up claude's behavior via hooks tooling or anything else, is mostly L4.'
share-the-setup-with-the-team.authors_note: The field has no settled name for this. The vocabulary's moves are about one agent's context, not a team's.

ladder_short.L2: Passes tips and rules to teammates by hand
ladder_short.L3: Commits the team's rules to the repo and keeps personal ones local
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that delivers the setup to every teammate

share-the-setup-with-the-team.entry_rules: 1: about 9 people in calls set up alone (173-call review) plus the tool-to-tool copying pitfall; 2: deciding what is shared versus personal is the person's act; 3: their team's repos, not an agent product.

keep-always-loaded-small.name: Trim, merge and retire the instructions that load every time
keep-always-loaded-small.what_you_do: They cut what the agent can work out without being told, merge rules that overlap, settle rules that contradict each other, reword a 'don't' into what to do instead, and retire a rule once its cause is fixed. When a written rule still gets ignored, they find out why: the file is too long, the rule is ambiguous or contradicted, or the code itself leads the agent the other way. Then they fix that cause instead of writing it louder.

ladder.L2: Trims or rewrites the file now and then, when it bites: after the agent ignored it, or after someone pointed at its size.
ladder.L3: What loads every time stays small over time. They can say why each line is there, they retire rules once the cause is fixed, and their trims hold instead of growing back. When a rule is ignored, they look for the cause in the rules or the code, not for louder wording.
ladder.L4: Built a check that keeps the files in shape without them: size limits, dead or duplicate rules, contradictions.

techniques.how: /context to see what loads every turn and how big it is.
techniques.laptop_signal: Words of instructions loaded at the start of each session (median, top tenth, largest)

techniques.how: Delete lines the agent follows anyway, move detail behind a reference, and keep one copy of each rule.
techniques.laptop_signal: Git history of instruction files: trims, where the removed lines went, files that grew back

techniques.how: Write rules as what to do, with the reason, and keep emphasis for a rule that is actually being skipped. Put what matters most at the start or the end.
A regular review that compares the rules with recent sessions to find rules that were ignored, corrections not yet captured, and stale entries.
A hook or CI check that fails when an instruction file passes a size limit or repeats a rule.
techniques.laptop_signal: Own hooks, decided by git (what each one checks is not read)

keep-always-loaded-small.call_evidence: 'When did you last delete a line from your rules file, and why?' and 'Is there a rule the agent keeps breaking anyway? What did you try?' L3 when they name a retired rule and its cause, or a fix for an ignored rule that wasn't louder wording. Ruling 6 is parked: ask this, but don't require it for Level 3 yet.
keep-always-loaded-small.laptop_evidence: Size of what loads at the start of each session, and the git history of the files they wrote: trims, splits, lines moved to docs or skills, and whether trimmed files grew back. The logs can't show whether a rule is ignored or contradicts another one.
