rulings: Ruling 6, parked ('later'): whether a Level 3 must show pruning. Ask it on calls; decide later.
Level guide row 6 note: an ignored rule is a context problem, not a cue to write a hook ('Stop saying a written rule gets ignored = it becomes a hook. Nobody's doing that.').
keep-always-loaded-small.authors_note: Merges context pruning (of the standing instructions), the smallest set of high-signal tokens, and consolidation and dead-clause audits.

ladder_short.L2: Trims the file now and then, when it bites
ladder_short.L3: File stays small over time; can say why each line exists
ladder_short.L4: Built a check for size, dead and duplicate rules

let-the-agent-fetch.name: Let the agent fetch what it needs from where it lives
let-the-agent-fetch.what_you_do: They don't paste tickets, logs, docs or whole files into the session. They leave the agent pointers (paths, links, a notes store) and let it look things up when it needs them. Context is any knowledge the agent works from: project facts, conventions, the best practices they follow.

ladder.L2: Points the agent at the files, folder or source in each session, or hands it the real evidence themselves (the error, the payload, a screenshot).
ladder.L3: Told the agent once where its knowledge lives (a docs folder, decision records, a notes vault they shaped). It then searches there without being asked ('search the vault first'). Connections others built are a Level 1 basic, not this level.
ladder.L4: Built the retrieval itself: their own connector, MCP server or search tool that changes what the agent can reach. A test shows it finds the right thing.

techniques.how: Name file paths or folders in the ask, and the agent reads them itself.
techniques.laptop_signal: Prompt names a file (English word list)

techniques.how: MCP servers or command-line tools others built, for tickets, logs, databases and docs.
techniques.laptop_signal: Outside tool servers used, and about 19 outside tools run from the shell

techniques.how: A line in the always-loaded file that says where knowledge lives and to search there first.
Their own MCP server or search index over the team's docs or notes.

let-the-agent-fetch.call_evidence: 'Where did the information for your last task come from, and how did it reach the agent?' L3 when they set up the place once and the agent searches it unprompted. L2 when they point at it or paste it each time. Using a connection someone else set up is the Level 1 basic.
let-the-agent-fetch.laptop_evidence: Tool servers and shell tools used, and whether prompts name files or paste errors. Whether the agent searched a store on its own because the setup says so is not separated today; the notes check catches some of it as sessions that start by reading notes.

learn.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

rulings: Ruling 10: 'A knowledge store whose shape they chose, which the agent is set up to search on its own, is engineered context, whatever it holds. Telling the agent once where its knowledge lives is setting it up; pointing it at a file in every session is Level 2.'
Ruling 7: 'MCP servers are not necessarily L4. Using them is a L1 basic thing. building them is a L4.'
Level guide: 'Pointing Claude at the right file is Level 2.'
let-the-agent-fetch.authors_note: Merges just-in-time context retrieval (agentic search, pulling instead of pushing) and RAG as a context fix.

ladder_short.L2: Points the agent at files, or pastes the real evidence
ladder_short.L3: Told it once where knowledge lives; it searches there itself
ladder_short.L4: Own MCP server or search tool; a test shows it finds things

compact-on-purpose.name: Compact a long session on purpose, saying what must survive
compact-on-purpose.what_you_do: Between steps, and before the session fills, they have the agent summarise the session so far and carry on from that summary. They tell it what must survive: the files, the decisions, the open question. They don't leave it to the automatic compaction at the edge of the window. They know a summary loses things, so what matters for longer lives in files.

ladder.L2: Compacts the session by hand at a point they choose and says what to keep. Watches how full the session is.
ladder.L3: Their setup decides what survives a compaction: standing instructions for what a summary must keep, and rules and state that reload from files afterwards, so a compaction loses nothing that matters.
ladder.L4: Built hooks or a program that save the state before a compaction and load it back after, or that compact at a threshold they set. A test shows it works.

techniques.how: /compact with focus instructions ('keep the file list and the open decisions').
techniques.laptop_signal: Compactions by hand compared with automatic ones, and how full the session was each time

techniques.how: A status line that shows how full the context is.
techniques.laptop_signal: Status line set

techniques.how: Compaction instructions in the always-loaded file; automatic compaction switched off.
Use only part of a big window even when it's switched on: compact or hand off well before the limit.
techniques.laptop_signal: How full the session was at each compaction (median)

techniques.how: Hooks before a compaction and at the session start that follows it, to save and reload the state.
techniques.laptop_signal: Hooks by event, and own hooks, decided by git

techniques.how: For people building agents: context editing in the API, which clears old tool calls and results.

compact-on-purpose.call_evidence: Ask what they do when a session gets long, and what they make sure survives. L2 when they compact it at a point they chose and name what to keep. Letting the automatic compaction carry a long session, or compacting again and again, is the Level 1 picture. Level 2, carried into Level 3.
compact-on-purpose.laptop_evidence: Compactions by hand compared with automatic ones, how full the session was when they happened, and stepping in before and after a compaction compared with the same points in sessions never compacted. Files carried into a compacted session are in the logs but not read yet.

rulings: Level guide row 10: 'They keep going, and compact again and again' is the Level 1 line.
Ruling 3: Level 2, carried into Level 3.
compact-on-purpose.authors_note: Merges compaction, anchored iterative summarization (a summary with fixed sections that is updated, not rewritten) and tool result clearing (dropping old tool output first).

ladder_short.L2: Compacts by hand at a chosen point, says what to keep
ladder_short.L3: Standing instructions decide what survives; state reloads from files
ladder_short.L4: Hooks save and reload state around compaction; a test shows it

design-the-context-you-send.name: Design the context your own agent sends the model
design-the-context-you-send.what_you_do: For an agent they build, they decide the format of what goes to the model, rather than a default session transcript. They do it for information density, error handling and cost. They keep a stable opening with history that is only appended to, so the cache keeps hitting. They mask tools instead of adding or removing them mid-run.

ladder.L4: Their agent builds its own context format (stable opening, append-only history, errors condensed), and they measure cache hits and quality with evals.

techniques.how: Agent SDK or API: their own message format, prompt-caching breakpoints and a fixed prefix.
techniques.laptop_signal: Scripts they wrote that start agents (what they send the model is not read)

techniques.how: Mask tool choices while the model writes its answer, or use a fixed set of tool states, instead of changing the tool list mid-run.

design-the-context-you-send.call_evidence: Ask only someone who builds agents: 'Show me what your agent actually sends the model on one turn, and why it's shaped that way.'
design-the-context-you-send.laptop_evidence: Scripts or programs they wrote that start agents. What those send the model is not read.

design-the-context-you-send.authors_note: Merges own your context window, design around the KV-cache, and mask, don't remove.

ladder_short.L4: Their own agent's context format, measured with evals

agent-managed-memory.name: Build your agent's memory as a curated store it updates in small edits
agent-managed-memory.what_you_do: For an agent they build, memory is a system. It can be an evolving playbook updated by small, structured edits after each run instead of being rewritten whole. It can be tiers of fast and slow memory that the agent moves data between. It can be work done ahead of time between requests.

ladder.L4: Their agent keeps and curates its own memory across runs by a mechanism they built, and evals show the memory helps rather than drifts.

techniques.how: Small updates to a playbook file after each run, with a separate step that curates it.
Memory tiers: a small core kept in context, and an archive the agent searches.
A background job that prepares summaries or answers between sessions.
techniques.laptop_signal: Schedules and scripted runs

agent-managed-memory.call_evidence: Ask only someone who builds agents: 'How does your agent's memory change after a run, and how do you know it got better rather than worse?'
agent-managed-memory.laptop_evidence: Scheduled or scripted runs they wrote. What those runs do to memory is not read.
rulings: Level guide row 8: 'They build memory systems, which the program doesn't teach' is where Level 4 starts.
agent-managed-memory.authors_note: Merges ACE (evolving playbooks), virtual context management (MemGPT memory tiers) and sleep-time compute.

ladder_short.L4: Their agent curates its own memory; evals show it helps

long-input-in-pieces.name: Have your agent work through long input in pieces
long-input-in-pieces.what_you_do: For agents they build that face more input than works in one context, the model treats the input as something outside itself. It examines the input with code and calls itself on pieces of it. Or it branches into a subtask and folds the result back into a short summary.

ladder.L4: Their agent splits long input and calls itself on the pieces, or folds subtasks back into summaries, and they measure it against a single long context with evals.

techniques.how: The long input is a variable in a code environment the model can inspect, split, and call itself on.
Branch-and-return subtasks that keep only a short result (needs a model trained for it).

long-input-in-pieces.call_evidence: Ask only someone who builds agents: 'What does your agent do when the input is bigger than its context can handle well?'
rulings: L4 needs building that changes how the agent runs, plus evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces 10-09/10-13).
long-input-in-pieces.authors_note: Merges RLMs and context folding (which needs a model trained for it).

ladder_short.L4: Their agent splits long input; evals compare it to one pass

bound-the-task.name: Hand over a bounded task: where it is, what done means, what to leave alone
bound-the-task.what_you_do: Before handing work over they say what to do, where it lives, why, how to tell it is done and what to leave alone, and they give the real error, log or output rather than their summary of it. The size of the task is set by what matters, not by a rule of one task per chat; a big task is split, proven on one piece, then finished.

ladder.L1: They hand over a wish and learn where the agent worked and when it decided it was done only by reading the result.
ladder.L2: Each ask names the task, where it lives, what done looks like and what to leave alone, with the real error or output in it, typed by hand every time.
ladder.L3: A task template they wrote supplies those parts, so their next ask and a teammate's carry them without anyone retyping.
ladder.L4: They built their own step that turns a ticket into a bounded ask and sends back any ask missing the place or the finish line before it reaches the agent, keep tuning it as their tickets change, and rerunning past tickets through it checks that every part still comes out.

techniques.how: Write the ask in five parts: what, where, why, how to check it is done, what to leave alone.
techniques.laptop_signal: Share of typed asks that name a file or path, and share that say what 'done' looks like (scan.py prompts_naming_a_file, prompts_stating_done; the 'done' words are an English word list).

techniques.how: Paste the real error, stack trace, failing output or payload, or point to where the agent can read it, instead of describing it.
techniques.laptop_signal: Share of typed asks that paste code or an error (scan.py prompts_with_code_or_error).

techniques.how: Ask the agent to list extras at the end instead of doing them, and to stop and report if the task turns out bigger than described.
For a big change, prove it on one piece first, then ask for the rest.
Have another model draft the brief from the ticket, then edit it before handing it over (still L2: they carry it).
@-mention the files the task is about.
techniques.laptop_signal: @-mentions count as naming a file (scan.py PATH_RE).

techniques.how: /goal with the finish line as the condition it works toward.
A slash command or skill they wrote that turns a ticket into the five-part ask (L3).
techniques.laptop_signal: Own skills and commands, decided by git (scan-coverage table 1, 'What they built'). What they do is not read.

bound-the-task.call_evidence: Read me the last thing you handed the agent, word for word. How did it know where to work and when it was finished?
bound-the-task.laptop_evidence: The scan reads prompt length, the share of asks that name a file, paste an error or say what 'done' means (English word list), and /goal use. The v13 reading of this practice is stuck at 'partly' for everyone (scan-coverage table 6). On the one laptop read (goal_drift.py), sessions that set out 'done' first had 4.5% early step-ins against 4.9% for the rest, with the project and session length held fixed. No payoff shows there yet. An L3 template shows only as 'an own skill or command', not as what it asks for. history.jsonl, which holds every typed prompt, is not read.
rulings: Level guide, not in the map: 'Pointing Claude at the right file is Level 2.'
Ruling 4: writing your own skills is "L3". A task-template skill or command they wrote is the L3 level. One someone else wrote is a basic: "Using them is a L1 basic thing."
L4 needs building that changes how the agent runs, plus evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces 10-09/10-13).
A practice that wasn't asked about is the interviewer's choice of where to stop, never a gap (11-02).

practice_card.title: Give it the evidence, not your summary of it
practice_card.text: Be explicit enough that the agent doesn't have to guess: the screenshot, the logs, the failing output, or a precise description of the behaviour when nothing else shows it. Point it at where to read more instead of pasting it all.

bound-the-task.authors_note: No vocabulary term names this move. It merges the vocabulary's fixes for overeagerness ('a minimal-solution prompt', 'state the boundaries: mention extras at the end instead of doing them', 'a stop-and-report prompt') and for fighting the weights ('smaller task steps'), the playbook's 'invocation quality', and v13's prompt-precision cues (exact location, one task, technical wording, scope limits).

ladder_short.L2: Spells out where, what done means and what to avoid each time
ladder_short.L3: Writes a task template that bounds every ask, theirs or a teammate's
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a step that turns tickets into bounded asks

bound-the-task.entry_rules: 1 seen: pr-narrow-brief 15/36, pr-point-location 8/36 · 2 a person writes the ask · 3 their own work.

settle-the-approach-first.name: Agree what to build and how before code, when the change is big enough to need it
settle-the-approach-first.what_you_do: Before a bigger change they have the agent explain the code they don't know, ask its questions and propose a plan, and they push back until the loose ends are covered. The agreed plan is what the work is held to. They skip this for a small fix; knowing when it is worth it is the skill, not planning every time.

ladder.L1: On a bigger change they say go, or skim the plan and approve it, and find the design they disagree with in the diff.
ladder.L2: Before a bigger change they work the approach through with the agent and change the plan before any code, and can say what they changed; they skip it for small fixes.
ladder.L3: The agreed plan or spec is a file the next session and their teammates work from and keep current, so the approach outlives the chat it was made in.
ladder.L4: They built their own step that turns a ticket into a spec with the open questions answered before code starts, without anyone running it by hand, keep tuning it as changes go wrong in new ways, and checking it on past changes that went wrong shows it would have caught them.

techniques.how: Type 'plan this first, no code yet, ask me your questions first'; this counts the same as any planning mode.
techniques.laptop_signal: A /plan command near the start (goal_drift.py 'goal_or_plan_command'). The typed words themselves are not read.

techniques.how: In code they don't know, have the agent explain how it works and where things live, check that against the code, then ask for the change.
techniques.laptop_signal: The agent read or searched before its first code edit (scan.py explored_before_first_edit).

techniques.how: Write the spec as a file before code: in scope, out of scope, the files, the existing pattern to copy, an example of the shape wanted.
techniques.laptop_signal: A plan, spec, brief or handoff file named in the first message (goal_drift.py 'names_a_plan_file').

techniques.how: Treat a first pass as exploration, then say 'scrap that and build it cleanly' with what was learned.
Plan mode: nothing is edited until they approve; decline the plan with feedback to send it back.
Spec tools someone else built are a basic (L1 per ruling 4); the practice is the spec and the push-back.

settle-the-approach-first.call_evidence: Show me a plan or spec from a recent bigger change. Where did you disagree with it, and what did you change before code was written?
settle-the-approach-first.laptop_evidence: The scan reads the plan-mode share, a /plan command near the start, a plan file named in the first message, and whether the agent explored before its first edit. Not read yet: whether they pushed back on a plan (plan_mode_reentry, declined plan dialogs) and the plan text in ~/.claude/plans/. On the one laptop read, plan-mode sessions had 6.0% early step-ins against 4.7% without, so plan mode is no sign on its own. Sessions that named a plan file had none (0 of 44 messages, only 8 sessions). Whether the next session works from the plan file is not read either; that is the context discipline's 'starts from zero' reading.
rulings: Ruling 8: "Why do we teach plan-first development in L3? It doesn't make sense". Planning first is a Level 2 habit.
10-27: "everybody plans work. I think our focus shouldn't be on plan driven strategies." Planning or plan mode alone reads no level.
SCOPE: plan mode is one way to plan; typing 'plan this' counts the same.
Ruling 11: dynamic workflows (ultracode) are L2. Building your own program that walks the plan is L4.
Using a spec tool or plugin someone else wrote is a basic ("Using them is a L1 basic thing"); the practice is the spec itself.

practice_card.title: On bigger changes, settle the approach before any code
practice_card.text: Planning still pays on larger work; the skill is knowing when. Many changes or unfamiliar code: plan first. A one-line fix: don't. Keep the agent from editing while you plan (plan mode, or a read-only ask mode), let it ask its questions, push back on the plan, then build in steps you can read.

settle-the-approach-first.authors_note: Merges spec-driven development (a structured spec as the source of truth for them and the agent) with plan mode, which is one technique among several. The vocabulary says both fix 'solving the wrong problem', which has no entry of its own, and vibe coding. Ruling 10-27: planning alone is what everybody does. What reads a level is the push-back and where the plan lives afterwards.

ladder_short.L2: Works the plan through with the agent before bigger changes
ladder_short.L3: Saves the agreed plan as a file later sessions and teammates follow
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a step that settles the spec before code

settle-the-approach-first.entry_rules: 1 seen: pr-plan-first 15/36, pr-spec-doc 10/36 · 2 a person agrees the plan · 3 their own work.

reword-the-ask.name: Name what went wrong and change the words that caused it
reword-the-ask.what_you_do: When the result is wrong or heads off course, they stop it, name exactly what is wrong and what the agent wasn't told, and change the ask: add the missing fact, give the reason for the rule, say what to do instead of what not to do, make the step smaller or vary the example. When the same miss repeats, they rewrite the template or standing instruction that caused it and remove what the fix replaces, instead of adding another line.

ladder.L1: They regenerate, repeat it louder or fix it quietly by hand, and the same miss comes back next time.
ladder.L2: Each time it misses they stop it, name the defect and what it wasn't told (or branch the chat and ask which instruction led it there), and reword what caused it.
ladder.L3: When a miss repeats, they rewrite the template or standing instruction that caused it and cut what the fix replaces, so the next session and a teammate don't hit it.
ladder.L4: They built their own tooling that traces each repeated miss to the part of the hand-over that caused it and proposes the fix at the source without them digging, keep refining it as new misses appear, and the asks that used to fail run as cases that show the fix holds.

techniques.how: Send it back with the defect named: what is wrong, where, and what it wasn't told.
techniques.laptop_signal: Corrections (English word list that catches about 7%; scan.py CORRECTION_RE). Corrections repeated within 5 messages, and what followed (context_poisoning.py).

techniques.how: Plain wording plus the reason instead of capitals and MUST; say what to do instead of what not to do.
When it keeps resisting, make the step smaller, reshape the ask, or try another model.
Give two or three varied examples and say what must stay the same, instead of one example it will copy.
Esc to stop it mid-run, or reject the tool call and type the reason.
/rewind or fork the session to before the wrong turn and reword, instead of piling corrections on top; in the fork, ask which instruction made it do that.
Edit the command, skill or agent file they wrote at the line that caused the miss, and delete what it replaces.

reword-the-ask.call_evidence: Tell me about the last time the agent got it wrong. What did you say back, and what in your own ask had caused it?
reword-the-ask.laptop_evidence: The scan reads corrections (English list, about 7% caught and 0 of 20 once translated), Esc and tool calls they rejected, runs of corrections and what followed. On the one laptop read (context_poisoning.py), 19 of 445 sessions had two corrections within 5 messages, and only 2 of those were followed by starting over. Not read yet: the words given with a refusal (userFeedback), which are the defect named in the moment; the wording of kept prompts (capitals, 'don't'); and the rewrite history of skills and sub-agent instructions. The v13 reading is stuck at 'ask' for everyone (scan-coverage table 6).
rulings: Ruling 4: writing your own skills is "L3". Kept prompts rewritten in place are the L3 level.

Ruling 5: a Claude-written rules file counts "if the way it writes CLAUDE.mds is supervised and doesn't just grow into context rot / pollution". The same test applies to kept prompts the agent edits for them.

Level guide row l3-s-06: an ignored rule is a wording or context problem, not a cue for a hook ("Stop saying a written rule gets ignored = it becomes a hook. Nobody's doing that."). So L4 here is evals, not a hook.
L4 needs evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces the 10-09/10-13 'evals the agent can't edit').
'Right altitude' is a single-source term: it names this practice but never anchors a level (README rule 1).
reword-the-ask.authors_note: Merges right altitude (between brittle hard rules and vague guidance; explain why a rule exists; a few varied examples instead of a list of edge cases) with several of the vocabulary's fixes: 'normal wording plus the reason' (aggressive prompt language), 'state what to do instead' (Pink Elephant), 'smaller task steps' (fighting the weights), 'diverse examples' (few-shotted), 'prune and rewrite the prompt instead of appending' and 'one patch per run' (whack-a-mole), and 'dead-clause audits' and 'treat prompts as perishable' (prompt debt). It also takes in v13's prompt accountability.

ladder_short.L2: Stops the agent, names what went wrong, and rewords the ask
ladder_short.L3: Rewrites the saved template or instruction behind a repeated miss
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that traces repeated misses to their cause

reword-the-ask.entry_rules: 1 seen: pr-name-defect 12/36, pr-own-wording 4/36 · 2 a person rewords · 3 their own work.

ask-without-leading.name: Ask without giving away the answer you hope for
ask-without-leading.what_you_do: They describe the symptom, not their guess, and ask for options or the case against before choosing. They treat quick agreement as a reason to check, not as confirmation. A sceptical-reviewer stance helps; a role on its own ('act as an expert') does not count.

ladder.L1: They put their guess in the question and take the agent's agreement as proof.
ladder.L2: Each time they give the symptom without their guess, ask for options or the case against, and check again when it agrees too fast.
ladder.L3: Their standing instructions tell every session to disagree with evidence, give options and say when it is unsure, so they don't have to ask.
ladder.L4: They built their own hand-over step so a guess never reaches the agent as fact, it works without them remembering to phrase things carefully, they keep tuning it as their work changes, and a test with a planted wrong guess shows the agent still pushes back.

techniques.how: Describe the symptom and ask for possible causes before naming yours.
Ask for options with trade-offs, or 'three ways this could break', before choosing.
Give the agent a sceptical-reviewer stance; a role alone is not counted.
A line in CLAUDE.md, or a reviewer sub-agent they wrote, telling it to push back with evidence and flag what it is unsure of (L3).
techniques.laptop_signal: Own agents and skills, by git (scan-coverage table 1). Their wording is not read.

ask-without-leading.call_evidence: When the agent agrees with you, how do you know it isn't just agreeing?
ask-without-leading.laptop_evidence: Nothing is read today. The logs carry the agent's replies, so 'agrees right after the person pushes back, then undoes its own work' could be counted. Standing instructions and reviewer sub-agents show up only as files, not their wording.
rulings: Using a reviewer plugin or skill someone else wrote is L1 ("Using them is a L1 basic thing"). A reviewer sub-agent or standing instruction they wrote is L3 (ruling 4).
A practice that wasn't asked about is never a gap (11-02).
ask-without-leading.authors_note: No vocabulary term names the move. The vocabulary lists it only as a fix: 'neutral prompt phrasing without your own opinion' for sycophancy, and 'gathering hints from comprehensive angles' for anchoring bias. Role prompting (persona prompting) merges in as one technique. There is no L4 level: the built version (a reviewer that never sees their opinion, or evals) is verification's generator/evaluator loop.

ladder_short.L2: Gives the symptom, not their guess, and asks for the case against
ladder_short.L3: Tells every session, in standing instructions, to push back with evidence
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a step that keeps guesses out of asks

ask-without-leading.entry_rules: 1 seen: L1/L2 answers on calls ('it agreed with me'; 'be critical, push back') · 2 a person asks · 3 their own work.

prove-it-works.name: Make the agent show it works before it says done
prove-it-works.what_you_do: Before the work starts, name the outcome that proves it (an end-to-end run, a migration on a local copy, the screen working). Then have the agent show that outcome, not its word: the real run and its output, or a test seen failing before and passing after. Pick the proof that fits the change; a count of tests is not the point.

ladder.L1: They take the agent's 'done' or 'all tests pass' at its word.
ladder.L2: Each time, they name the outcome that proves the work and have the agent show it with its output, checking each step's result before the next on risky work and sending back any test the agent weakened.
ladder.L3: Their setup makes the agent show proof without being asked: the project's written rules say what proves a change here and how to run it, the agent can run and see the product, and checks run on every change, so a teammate's session does the same.
ladder.L4: They built their own gate (a check, a hook or a runner) that won't let work count as done until a check a script decides has passed, so unattended work proves itself, keep tuning the checks as their work changes, and re-running it on past false 'done's shows it still catches them.

techniques.how: Test first: the agent writes the test, runs it and shows it failing, then makes it pass. Tell it to report a wrong test, never change it to pass.
techniques.laptop_signal: A test, build or lint run after the agent's last edit and before the commit (comprehension_debt.py, checks.py). The fail-then-pass order is not read.

techniques.how: A quick live try (a spike) instead of a permanent test when the change doesn't need one to stay.
techniques.laptop_signal: 'Ran a file it changed' or 'ran a script of the project' after the last edit (comprehension_debt.py)

techniques.how: Give the agent eyes: let it run the app, call the endpoint, drive a browser or terminal, and show what it saw.
techniques.laptop_signal: 'Ran the app' after the last edit: curl, localhost, browser automation, screenshots (comprehension_debt.py)

techniques.how: Lines in the project CLAUDE.md saying how to run and read the checks here and that a passing run must be shown before handing back.
techniques.laptop_signal: checks.py 'who made the check happen': the repo's instructions say to

techniques.how: /goal with a condition the agent must meet before it stops.
techniques.laptop_signal: /goal and its status in the session logs (scan, Sessions row)

techniques.how: Only for unattended runs (claude -p, Agent SDK, a loop script): a Stop hook or runner step that runs a check a script can decide and blocks the finish while it fails. Not as the definition of done in a session someone is watching (his ruling, 10-16).
CI or pre-commit checks on every change, with the agent told to read their result.

prove-it-works.call_evidence: The agent says 'done, all tests pass'. What do you look at before you believe it? Tell me about a time it wasn't true.
prove-it-works.laptop_evidence: Share of code commits with a test, build, lint or a run of the app after the agent's last edit (comprehension_debt.py, checks.py). Who made the check happen: the person asked (L2), the repo's instructions (L3), a hook or program they wrote (L4). Refusals by checks they wrote, and whether the next try passed: on one laptop, 237 refusals in 30 days, 228 in runs nobody was typing in, and 43 of 82 blocked runs passed on the next try (no_backpressure.py). After a failed check, whether the next step was a fix and a green re-run or a changed test file (checks.py). Not seen: tests run by CI or git hooks, output read in the editor, the fail-then-pass order.
rulings: 'Either a good testing strategy, or no testing at all (prefer spiking)' (10-29): the level comes from the proof chosen for the change, never from how many tests exist.

A check they wrote that refuses 'done' is this practice's top level only in runs nobody watches and only when a script can decide the outcome (10-16 hooks norm). Building it counts toward building (ruling 2: 'mostly L4'), but the level needs an eval (11-02: 'an eval, period').
Running a checking hook or plugin someone else wrote is L1: 'Using them is a L1 basic thing.' Credit goes to whoever wrote the script (git).

practice_card.title: Name the outcome that proves it, then ask for that proof
practice_card.text: Before the work starts, say what result shows it is done: an end-to-end run, a migration that succeeds on a local copy, a preview you can click through. Ask for that result and its real output.

prove-it-works.authors_note: Vocabulary moves merged here: backpressure; TDD with agents (write the failing test first, see it fail, then make it pass); 'audit each progress claim against a tool result'; 'verify packages exist before install'; 'a prompt asking for a general solution and to flag incorrect tests instead of working around them'; hidden or holdout tests at the top level (dropped from the level text by the 11-02 ruling: L4 needs an eval, whether the agent can edit it is not part of any level).

ladder_short.L2: Names the proof and has the agent show it each time
ladder_short.L3: Writes down what proves a change, so every session shows it unasked
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a gate that blocks 'done' until checks pass

prove-it-works.entry_rules: False 'done' is the most common verification story on calls (l2-s-08); asking for proof is a person's habit; it is about their own work.

second-look.name: Have the work checked by a reviewer that didn't write it
second-look.what_you_do: Before taking the work further, have it checked by something that never saw how it was made and can only read, not fix. Ask it what's wrong, then judge each finding yourself instead of passing it on.

ladder.L1: The agent that wrote the work is the only one that checks it, and it says it's fine.
ladder.L2: Each time, they hand the changes to a fresh session or a separate read-only reviewer, ask what's wrong, and judge each finding themselves.
ladder.L3: Their setup gives every change a second look before a pull request without them remembering: a reviewer they set up, with what to look for and read-only access, that their usual flow calls.
ladder.L4: They built their own reviewer whose verdict decides when work moves on, with a cap on rounds, so it runs without them, keep tuning what it looks for as their work changes, and re-running it on past changes with known bugs shows it still finds them.

techniques.how: Paste the changes into a fresh session that never saw the work, ask what's wrong, judge each point.
A reviewer subagent in .claude/agents with read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob), started before a pull request with a short brief.
techniques.laptop_signal: Review sub-agents started after the last edit and before a commit (comprehension_debt.py 'review sub-agent'; scan: sessions with a review step); agents they wrote, credited by git

techniques.how: A workflow with a build step and a separate verify step that only reads.
techniques.laptop_signal: Workflow runs are counted; what runs inside them is not read

techniques.how: The team's AI review bot on pull requests, each comment judged before acting on it.

second-look.call_evidence: Who or what checks the agent's work besides the session that wrote it? Tell me one thing that check caught that would have shipped.
second-look.laptop_evidence: Review sub-agents started after the last edit and before a commit or pull request (comprehension_debt.py, scan); reviewer agents or skills they wrote, credited by git; refusals by a reviewer step inside a hook or runner they wrote (no_backpressure.py). Not seen: review on GitHub, a fresh session the changes were pasted into by hand, whether they judged the findings.
rulings: Using a review plugin or bot someone else wrote is L1 ('Using them is a L1 basic thing'). Calling it on each change and judging what it finds is the L2 act, the same as a fresh session.
A reviewer agent or skill they wrote is L3 (writing your own skills: 'L3').
Running a dynamic workflow that has a review phase is L2 (ruling 11: 'it's an L2 thing'). Building their own program that runs builder and reviewer is L4.

practice_card.title: Get a second look from a reviewer that didn't write it
practice_card.text: Review in a brand-new session, with a different model, or with a read-only reviewer agent given a short brief ('find what is wrong, do not fix'). Let the coding agent resolve the comments in a loop, cap the rounds (three), and keep a human on the decision. Judge each finding yourself. It works especially well on front-end work.

second-look.authors_note: Vocabulary moves merged here: generator/evaluator loop, evaluator-optimizer, Writer/Reviewer pattern, verification subagent, fresh-context reviewer, adversarial review step.

ladder_short.L2: Hands changes to a fresh, read-only reviewer and judges each finding
ladder_short.L3: Sets up a reviewer that checks every change before a pull request
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a reviewer whose verdict gates the work

second-look.entry_rules: Fires on 24/92 calls with v13's strongest verification signal (0.38); a person chooses and judges the review; own work.

own-what-ships.name: Read, run and be able to explain what ships
own-what-ships.grade: standard (cognitive psychology since 2016; for AI its meaning is split: healthy delegation or over-reliance)
own-what-ships.what_you_do: Hand over the typing, keep the decision. Before agent work reaches a teammate or client, read the actual changes, run them as a user would, and be able to explain any part; if you can't explain it, it doesn't ship. Write the costly parts yourself (auth, money, data migrations) or read them line by line, and form your own view before taking the agent's advice.

ladder.L1: Agent work goes out once it looks right or the tests pass, and they can't say what it changed underneath.
ladder.L2: Before it reaches anyone, they read the changes, run them like a user and can explain any part, writing or reading line by line the parts where a mistake is costly.
ladder.L3: Their setup makes owning it the default: every agent change comes back with what changed, why, how it was proven and what to read first, in a format their teammates and reviewers also get.
ladder.L4: They built their own hand-back (what changed, why, how it was proven, what to read first) into how work leaves them so nothing reaches a reviewer without it, keep tuning it from what reviewers send back, and tracking those reverts shows unread work has stopped getting out.

techniques.how: Read all the changes before committing or opening a pull request; run the change yourself (click through it, call the API).
Ask the agent to quiz you on the change, and not to open the pull request until you can answer.
A standing hand-back format: what changed, why, how it was proven, what to look at first.
The Learning output style: the agent leaves parts for you to write and explains its choices.
techniques.laptop_signal: Output styles in use (scan: What the agent knows)

own-what-ships.call_evidence: Show me the last agent change you shipped. What did you check before it went out? Pick one function: what does it do?
own-what-ships.laptop_evidence: Changes shown after the last edit and before the commit; commits straight after an edit with nothing looked at, and whether a fix or revert followed within hours (checks.py, comprehension_debt.py); pull requests opened from sessions. Not seen today: reading in the editor, edits by hand (in the logs as files edited outside the agent and in file-history copies, unread), whether they understood any of it. v13's 'could defend every line' was always 'ask' on the laptop for this reason.
rulings: An unasked practice is the interviewer's choice of where to stop, never a gap (11-02). This practice is seen mostly on calls, so silence on the laptop is not L1.
L4 is null by design: understanding can't be built into machinery. Checks the agent can't skip belong to prove-it-works, second-look and retest-agent-setup.

practice_card.title: You own the architecture and the risky part; the agent fills in
practice_card.text: Decide structure, schema, library and the approach yourself, give the agent one finished example or reference, scope it to a folder, then delegate the repetitive or mechanical parts. For the most sensitive or judgement-heavy logic, write the pseudo-code or core yourself and have the agent write tests or sub-agents. Try alternative approaches yourself before accepting its first one. This is the platform work engineers have to engineer themselves.

own-what-ships.authors_note: The term is used only in the healthy sense (you keep the decision); many AI papers use it for the harmful kind. Vocabulary moves merged here: cognitive offloading; 'review the code before sharing it' (AI slop); 'own the diff: read it before you ask anyone to review it' and 'read it, understand it, validate it, then answer in your own words' (meat proxy); 'practise without the agent', 'coding without the agent on a schedule' and the conceptual-inquiry style of asking (skill atrophy, comprehension debt); 'keep forming an independent view' (cognitive surrender). The field's umbrella for this is agentic engineering: the AI implements, the human owns architecture, quality and correctness.

ladder_short.L2: Reads, runs and can explain changes before they reach anyone
ladder_short.L3: Gets every change back with what changed, why, and its proof
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a hand-back that no change can skip

own-what-ships.entry_rules: Reading before shipping fires on 60/92 calls and its absence on 11/92; only a person can own it; own work.

turn-misses-into-checks.name: Turn every defect that got through into a check that catches it next time
turn-misses-into-checks.what_you_do: When a defect in the agent's work gets past 'done', fix it and add the check that would have caught it, so the same kind of mistake fails next time in anyone's session. A defect in how the agent behaves goes into the agent's saved cases instead (see retest-agent-setup).

ladder.L1: The same kind of defect comes back, and they fix it by hand each time.
ladder.L2: When they catch a defect in the agent's work, they fix it and, when they remember, have the agent add a test that fails without the fix.
ladder.L3: Their setup does it every time: the project's rules say every fix comes with a check that fails without it, so the agent adds one in any session, theirs or a teammate's.
ladder.L4: They built their own step that turns each defect found after 'done' into a check that runs on every change without them, keep tuning it as the kinds of defect change, and their record shows that kind of defect has stopped coming back.

techniques.how: For each bug: reproduce it in a test, see the test fail, then fix; the test stays.
A line in the project CLAUDE.md: every fix ships with a test that fails without it.
A short log of defects caught after 'done', sorted by kind, read now and then to see which kinds still repeat.

turn-misses-into-checks.call_evidence: Tell me about a bug the agent made that you caught. What makes sure that one can't come back?

ladder_short.L2: Fixes each defect and, when they remember, adds a test for it
ladder_short.L3: Makes it a project rule that every fix comes with a check
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a step that turns escaped bugs into checks

turn-misses-into-checks.entry_rules: Defects caught on 51/92 calls with little said about keeping them caught; adding the check is a person's habit; own work.

retest-agent-setup.name: Re-test your agent setup on saved cases (evals) after every change
retest-agent-setup.what_you_do: When you change a prompt, a rule, or a reviewer or helper agent you set up, re-run a fixed set of cases and see whether it got better or worse, instead of trying it once. Build the cases from where the agent really went wrong: note each miss, sort them into kinds, and write cases for the kinds that matter. Grade with code where you can, and with a judging model checked against your own labels where you can't.

ladder.L1: They change a prompt, rule or helper agent, try it once, and call it fine.
ladder.L2: After each change they re-try the same few saved tasks in a fresh session and compare with what they got before.
ladder.L3: They keep a saved set of cases built from real misses, each with what a pass looks like, and a command anyone on the team can run re-checks the setup after a change.
ladder.L4: They built their own harness that runs a saved set of cases on every change to the setup without them, keep growing the cases from new misses, and a drop in the result blocks the change, which is the proof the setup still holds.

techniques.how: Cases in evals/<case>/case.yaml run with claude plugin eval, wired to a package.json script or Makefile target the team can call.
A CI job on every push or pull request that runs claude plugin eval and fails the change on a drop (no '|| true', no continue-on-error).
Run cases headless (claude -p or the Agent SDK) from a script, each in a fresh copy, and compare with the last run.
techniques.laptop_signal: Headless runs whose folder or command names an eval; eval commands; repos with an evals folder (scan.py; practices.py loop_23)

techniques.how: An eval tool such as promptfoo, Inspect, DeepEval or Braintrust.
techniques.laptop_signal: Eval tool names in shell commands (scan.py)

techniques.how: Read where the agent went wrong in real sessions, sort and count the misses, write cases for the kinds that matter.

retest-agent-setup.call_evidence: When you last changed a prompt, rule or helper agent, how did you know it didn't get worse? Name a case and what it checks.
retest-agent-setup.laptop_evidence: Automated eval runs and eval commands, and repos with an evals folder (scan.py, practices.py); eval runs inside sandbox copies (no_backpressure.py). Not seen: who can write the eval, whether a drop blocked anything, whether the cases came from real failures.
rulings: 'I think that to be an architect he needs to demonstrate architect things, including building any of tools, mcp, skills, and running evals' (10-13).
L4 needs evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces the 10-09/10-13 'evals the agent can't edit').
retest-agent-setup.authors_note: Vocabulary moves merged here: evals; error analysis (open and axial coding of real failures, single-source, so it names a step but never anchors a level); eval-driven development (write the eval before or with the change and gate on it); LLM-as-a-judge (a model grades open-ended output). People building agent products do the same thing at a larger scale. The can't-edit condition on the cases and grader was dropped from the level text by the 11-02 ruling.

ladder_short.L2: Reruns a few saved tasks by hand after each change
ladder_short.L3: Keeps cases from real misses and one command anyone can rerun
ladder_short.L4: Builds and grows evals that run on every change and block drops

retest-agent-setup.entry_rules: L4 overall needs an eval (10-13, 11-02) and laptops show setup edits without re-tests; a person runs them; only their own agent setup counts, not an AI feature they ship.

give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.name: Build tools for the agent, with short output, that reach the systems it needs
give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.what_you_do: When the agent keeps fumbling a command made for people, or can't reach the build, the ticket or the data so they paste it in, they give it a way in shaped for it: short output, plain errors, exactly the fields the task needs. They design what it can ask for and what it gets back, not only whether it can connect. Using connections someone else built is the everyday floor, not this practice.

ladder.L1: They paste logs, tickets and query results in by hand, or watch the agent wade through output made for people; connections others set up are used as they come.
ladder.L2: Each time the agent fumbles or can't reach something, they show it in the session which command or option fetches it with short, readable output, instead of pasting it in.
ladder.L3: They wrote small tools for the agent (a script or task command that fetches the build log, the ticket or the rows the task needs, with short output and plain errors), and their setup names them so every session and teammate uses them unasked.
ladder.L4: They built their own tools for the agent (command-line tools, scripts, servers, plugins) with commands and replies designed for it, so any system it needs is one call away with nobody pasting anything in, keep reshaping them as their work changes, and tests show they still work.

techniques.how: An MCP server they wrote, with tool names, inputs and replies shaped for the agent (L4)
A project script or task-runner command with short output and plain errors, named in the project's always-loaded instructions (L3)
Command-line clients for CI, tickets and the database (gh, the CI's CLI, a read-only query script) the agent calls instead of the person pasting
Their own plugin that adds tools or commands for the agent
techniques.laptop_signal: Plugins installed from a marketplace folder they keep

techniques.how: MCP servers and plugins others built, wired in: the L1 floor, not evidence of this practice

give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.call_evidence: Tell me about the last time you pasted something into the agent, a log, a ticket, a query result, or watched it get stuck on a command. Could it have fetched that itself, and what did you change?
give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.laptop_evidence: Connected services called per server and outside tools run from the shell show the floor. Not read yet: tool servers they wrote and scripts the agent calls (scan coverage, table 5: 'Building your own MCP server' has no check).
rulings: Ruling 7: 'MCP servers are not necessarily L4. Using them is a L1 basic thing. building them is a L4.'
Ruling 4: writing your own skills = L3. Small scripts written for the agent are read the same way here (our reading; to be confirmed).
L4 needs building that changes how the agent runs, plus evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces 10-09/10-13).
give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.authors_note: The floor is ruling 7: using connections others built.

ladder_short.L2: Shows the agent which command fetches the data, instead of pasting it
ladder_short.L3: Writes small agent tools that every session and teammate uses unasked
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests its own tools shaped for the agent

give-the-agent-tools-made-for-it.entry_rules: Credited only for a tool they shaped for the agent; using or wiring in someone else's connection is the L1 floor (ruling 7: 'Using them is a L1 basic thing. building them is a L4').

enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.name: Turn a rule that must always hold into a check that runs every time
enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.what_you_do: For a rule that must hold every time and always gives the same answer (never commit a secrets file, never force-push, format every file written), they stop asking in words and make a check that runs at that moment and blocks or fixes the action, whatever the agent was told. Words guide before the agent acts; a check catches the action as it happens. They keep checks for cheap fixed rules and hard gates, not for deciding when the work is done.

ladder.L1: A rule that must always hold lives only in the instructions; the agent breaks it now and then and they find out afterwards.
ladder.L2: They catch the breach themselves each time: look for it in the diff, undo the force-push, re-run the formatter, and remind the agent.
ladder.L3: A ready-made check is wired into the project (a secret scan before every commit, a formatter on every saved file), so the rule holds for every session and teammate without them.
ladder.L4: They wrote their own checks that block or fix the action the moment it happens, with nobody stepping in, keep a record of what each one stopped, keep tuning them as their rules and projects change, and a test shows each one still blocks.

techniques.how: A hook before a tool call that refuses a fixed-rule action (staging a secrets file, a force-push) by exiting with an error
techniques.laptop_signal: Hooks wired in user and project settings and switched-on plugins, credited by git authorship of the script; hooks that can block; blocks that fired

techniques.how: A hook after a file is written that formats or auto-fixes it every time
techniques.laptop_signal: Hooks wired on file writes, credited by git authorship

techniques.how: Their own plugin that carries their checks into every project
A git pre-commit or pre-push hook they wrote to check the agent's commits (level pending his ruling)
When the action is never allowed at all, a deny rule instead of a check (see 'Decide what the agent may do on its own')

enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.call_evidence: Which rule does your agent have to follow every single time, and what happens when it doesn't? What stops it, and when did that last fire?
enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.laptop_evidence: Checks wired in user and project settings and in switched-on plugins, credited by who wrote the script (git history); which can refuse; refusals that fired and whether the agent's next step changed (backpressure check: one laptop, 237 refusals in 30 days, 228 in runs without the person typing; 221 of the 237 are checks on 'done', which belong to verification, not to this practice). Missed today: refusals that come back as a tool result (issues log B18) and git pre-commit hooks.
rulings: His hooks norm (10-16): hooks are for 'a cheap rule that must hold every time', 'a hard gate on what can't be undone', 'the right context at the right moment', and 'watching, logging, notifying'. They are not for 'defining done', not for 'blocking on something cheap to redo, like a failing test', and not for 'replacing a person who is already reviewing'. "'If it matters, make it a hook' is wrong as a general rule… What counts is whether a hook was the right tool."
Ruling 2: 'Setting up claude's behavior via hooks tooling or anything else, is mostly L4. Engineering the behavior of agents through scripting (plugins) is l4'.
10-09: 'A plugin counts by what it does': an own plugin that alters the agent's runtime or behaviour counts as building; one that only bundles skills or commands is tooling.
Git hook written to check the agent's work: pending ruling (v13 h10-git-hook).
enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.authors_note: Merges: guardrails (standard); guides and sensors (single-source). Guides are the rules files and skills of context; sensors are verification's backpressure; a guard is the sensor that can refuse.

ladder_short.L2: Catches each breach by hand and reminds the agent
ladder_short.L3: Wires ready-made checks into the project, so they hold for everyone
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests their own checks that block a breach instantly

enforce-fixed-rules-in-code.entry_rules: Only checks for a fixed rule or an irreversible step count; a check that decides 'done' or re-runs the tests at every stop is verification, and he rejected it as a tip (hooks norm 10-16).

limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.name: Decide what the agent may do alone, what needs a person, and what's off-limits
limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.what_you_do: Before it works, they sort what the agent may touch and do: what goes through without asking (reading, editing on a branch, running tests), what waits for a person (a push, a deploy, a data write, a message to someone outside), and what stays out of reach (production keys, secrets, the admin database user). Where they want it to run with no questions, they first put it somewhere it can't do lasting harm, such as a throwaway copy or a container. They decide case by case per project; there is no one rule.

ladder.L1: Either every action asks and they click yes without reading, or they switched the questions off on a machine with their keys, client code and production in reach.
ladder.L2: They decide per task what the agent may touch, do the risky steps themselves, read the risky requests and say no when one is wrong, and commit or branch before letting it run loose.
ladder.L3: Their project settings sort it for every session and teammate: routine commands go through, pushes and data writes stop for a person, secrets and production are refused, and runs with no questions happen only inside a sandbox or container.
ladder.L4: They engineered their own boundary layer (short-lived keys for one job, a gate for actions that can't be undone, their own sandbox image) that every run starts inside, keep tightening it as projects change, and a test tries to get past it on every change, for example a planted fake secret never leaks.

techniques.how: Allow, ask and deny rules in the project's committed settings; deny rules hold in every permission mode, including with prompts off
Permission mode switched by task (ask, accept edits, plan, auto); bypass only inside a container, never on the host
The built-in sandbox: commands limited to the project folder and approved servers, chosen variables and files hidden
A dev container or virtual machine the agent always runs in; a commit or a separate working copy before a long run as the way back
Scoped keys: a read-only database user, a one-repo token, no production keys on the machine; protected branches on the remote
Never one run that holds private data, reads text outsiders wrote and can send things out: drop one of the three
A hook on permission requests that holds a chosen action for a person (written by them = L4)

limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.call_evidence: What won't you let the agent do on its own, and what stops it? When did you last say no to it, and why?
limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.laptop_evidence: Refuse and ask rules in user and project settings; headless runs started with tool or permission limits; which connections are on for every project vs per project. Not read yet: secrets in plain files the agent can open, which keys the agent's commands use, sub-agents' tool lists.
rulings: Level guide, draft Level 2 row 9 'What the agent doesn't get to do': L2 decides on purpose what the agent may touch and what they do by hand; L1 gives it the same reach for everything, or auto-approves to go faster; L4 starts with 'They build the guardrail so nobody's agent can do it.'
Level guide not_in_the_map: building 'guardrails and cost limits' is Level 4.
L4 needs building that changes how the agent runs, plus evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces 10-09/10-13).

practice_card.title: Limit what the agent can touch, and keep a way back
practice_card.text: Draw the boundary yourself: read-only database user, no production access, scoped credentials per directory, branch-from-latest-and-open-a-PR instructions, no commit without an approved message, plan-before-apply in CI. Work on a branch and commit each good step. Use a deny list or a hook for the hard rules, not a prompt alone.

limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.authors_note: Merges: least privilege for agents (standard); Agents Rule of Two (emerging: no more than two of the three in one session); 'remove one of the three legs' (the lethal trifecta's own fix). Its failure mode is OWASP's 'excessive agency'.

ladder_short.L2: Decides per task what the agent may touch, and does risky steps
ladder_short.L3: Keeps project settings that allow, ask about or refuse each action
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests its own boundary every run starts inside

limit-what-the-agent-can-reach.entry_rules: Credited for limits they set (settings, scoped keys, a box, a rollback point); the tool's default prompts, or access they simply don't have, don't count.

build-what-the-agent-runs-inside.name: Script how each agent run starts, so none is set up by hand
build-what-the-agent-runs-inside.what_you_do: Instead of setting up every run by hand (the right copy of the code, the same opening setup, the right helpers with the right tools and limits), they make the setup itself: agent roles with their own tools and model, a start command that brings each run up the same way, or a program that drives the agent and changes how it behaves. Every run starts ready, the same for them and for a teammate.

ladder.L1: Every run starts from scratch: they open a session, paste the same setup, pick the branch and the helpers by hand, and skip a step now and then.
ladder.L2: They follow their own routine by hand each time: a fresh branch or copy, the same opening instructions, the helpers they need started one by one.
ladder.L3: Their setup brings the run up: agent roles they wrote (what each does, its tools, its model) and a saved start command make every run start the same way, for them and a teammate.
ladder.L4: They wrote their own program that drives the agent or changes how it runs (starts and steers sessions, adds context or gates at set moments), it runs every session without them stepping in, they keep tuning it as their work changes, and a saved set of cases re-run after each change shows it still works.

techniques.how: Agent definition files they wrote, each with a role, a tool list and a model
Their own program on the Agent SDK, or headless runs from their own script, that start and steer sessions
Their own plugin whose hooks add context or gates at set moments, or that defines agents (counts by what it does to the run)
A start script that makes a separate working copy, loads the setup and launches the agent with its limits
An output style they wrote, replacing the agent's system prompt (supporting only)

build-what-the-agent-runs-inside.call_evidence: Walk me through how a run starts, from nothing to the agent working. Which of those steps did you build, and how do you know it still works after you change it?

ladder_short.L2: Repeats their setup routine by hand before every run
ladder_short.L3: Saves agent roles and a start command that bring every run up
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a program that drives and steers each session

build-what-the-agent-runs-inside.entry_rules: A plugin or program counts by what it does to the run (10-09); one that only bundles skills or commands is tooling, and when runs start (a schedule, an event) is orchestration.

run-the-agent-in-a-box.name: Run the agent inside a sandbox
run-the-agent-in-a-box.what_you_do: They let the agent work freely only inside walls. It can read and write only the project folder and reach only approved servers. The machine or container it runs in can be thrown away. That is a sandbox, and it is what makes running without permission prompts safe ('safe YOLO mode'). For damage to the code itself, a rollback point made before a long run does the same job: a commit, a branch or a separate copy.

ladder.L2: Before a risky or long run, makes the damage easy to undo by hand: commits or branches first, or runs it in a throwaway copy, container or virtual machine started for the job.
ladder.L3: Every session runs inside the boundary by default: the built-in sandbox switched on with the folders and servers it may reach, or a dev container the repo always opens in. Prompts are switched off only inside it.
ladder.L4: Built the sandbox: their own container image or wrapper script that starts the agent with no way out except what they allow. A planted fake secret never shows up, and a test checks it.

techniques.how: The built-in sandbox: shell commands limited to the project folder and approved servers, with sandbox.credentials hiding chosen variables and files
techniques.laptop_signal: 'sandbox' key present in settings (key names only). Commands marked sandboxed are in the logs but not read yet

techniques.how: A dev container or virtual machine the agent always runs in
techniques.laptop_signal: Repos with a .devcontainer folder

techniques.how: Bypass permissions only inside the container, never on the host
techniques.laptop_signal: Share of typed messages with all permission checks off; settings that skip the all-off mode's warning (read together with whether a box was in use)

techniques.how: A commit, a branch or a separate working copy before a long or unattended run, as a rollback point

run-the-agent-in-a-box.call_evidence: They say where risky or unattended runs happen (a container, a virtual machine, a throwaway copy) and what the agent can't reach from there. Or they say they commit or branch before letting it run loose (the rollback half of v13 hn-perm-scoped). L1: every prompt off, on their own laptop, with nothing around it.
run-the-agent-in-a-box.laptop_evidence: Sandbox switched on in settings; repos with a dev container; share of messages with all permission checks off, read against whether a box was in use. In the logs but not read yet: commands marked as sandboxed.

learn.title: Anthropic: Claude Code sandboxing (beyond permission prompts)

rulings: The vocabulary's YOLO mode entry quotes the Claude Code docs: bypass permissions is for 'isolated containers and VMs only'.

L4 needs evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces the 10-09/10-13 'evals the agent can't edit'). The playbook's canary-secret test (/setup/secrets-safety) is the shape of that eval for a box.
run-the-agent-in-a-box.authors_note: Merges: sandboxing (standard), container isolation, safe YOLO mode. AI boxing is an AI-safety term and is dropped (SCOPE).

ladder_short.L2: Commits first, or runs risky jobs in a throwaway copy
ladder_short.L3: Every session runs in the sandbox or a dev container
ladder_short.L4: Built their own sandbox image; a planted fake secret never leaks

ask-before-what-cant-be-undone.name: Ask a person only before steps that can't be undone
ask-before-what-cant-be-undone.what_you_do: Approval goes where it counts. Before a push, a deploy, a delete, a database write or a message to someone outside, the agent stops and a person reads what it is about to do. Steps that are cheap to redo (reading, editing on a branch, running tests) go through without asking, so the few questions left get real attention. Saying no, and why, is part of it.

ladder.L2: Reads each request on the risky steps and says no when it is wrong. Loosens or tightens how much the agent may do as the task changes: asks for everything on unfamiliar code, lets edits through on routine work.
ladder.L3: Their settings sort it for every session: routine commands go through, while pushes, deploys and data writes always stop for a person or are blocked. The few prompts left are worth reading.
ladder.L4: Built the approval gate: a check that holds actions that can't be undone (a push to the main branch, a production write, a message sent outside) until a person approves, for everyone's agent, with a test showing it can't be skipped.

techniques.how: Permission modes switched by task (ask, accept edits, plan, auto)
techniques.laptop_signal: Permission mode recorded on each typed message (share per mode)

techniques.how: Allow rules for routine commands; ask or deny rules for push, deploy and data writes
techniques.laptop_signal: Allow, ask and deny rule counts and the default mode in settings

techniques.how: Auto mode: a classifier approves routine actions and stops risky ones. Tool results are kept from the classifier, so hostile text can't sway it
techniques.laptop_signal: Share of typed messages in auto mode

techniques.how: A hook on permission requests or before tool calls that holds a chosen action for a person (written by them = L4)
techniques.laptop_signal: Hooks wired before tool calls, credited by git authorship; refusals that fired

techniques.how: Protected branches and required review on the remote, so a push can't land on its own

ask-before-what-cant-be-undone.call_evidence: They name the steps that always wait for them and the last time they said no, with the reason (level guide row 9 ask: 'What won't you let Claude do on its own, and why?'). They say routine steps go through, so prompts are rare. L1: 'I just click yes', or switched prompts off to stop the waiting.
ask-before-what-cant-be-undone.laptop_evidence: Permission mode on each typed message; allow, ask and deny counts and the default mode; minutes agents wait on the person (waiting check). In the logs but not read yet: tool calls the person rejected (toolDenialKind user-rejected), the plainest sign prompts are read. Permission prompts themselves leave no record.

learn.title: Anthropic: beyond permission prompts (approval fatigue, 93% accepted)

rulings: Level guide, draft Level 2 row 9: 'They decide on purpose what the agent may touch and what they do by hand: no direct database access, no auto-approve on anything shared.' L1 there: 'auto-approve to go faster'.
An unasked practice is the interviewer's choice of where to stop, never a gap (11-02).
ask-before-what-cant-be-undone.authors_note: Merges: human-in-the-loop (standard) with two fixes the vocabulary lists for approval fatigue, permission allow-lists and classifier-gated approvals (the latter is a technique).

ladder_short.L2: Reads risky requests and says no; adjusts permissions per task
ladder_short.L3: Settings let routine commands through; pushes and deploys stop
ladder_short.L4: Built an approval gate for everyone's agent; a test can't skip it

vet-what-gets-in.name: Check plugins, MCP servers and dependencies before they get in
vet-what-gets-in.what_you_do: Every plugin, skill or MCP server someone else wrote puts its author's words into the agent's instructions, and every package the agent suggests runs someone else's code. Before installing, they read what it will tell the agent or run, check that a suggested package really exists and is the one they meant, and keep the list of what is switched on short and known.

ladder.L2: Before installing a plugin someone else wrote, reads what it will tell the agent or run. When the agent adds a package, looks it up before it is installed.
ladder.L3: Their setup keeps it checked for them and their teammates: a short list of approved plugins in the project's rules, versions pinned, and every new package visible in review through the file that pins versions. Nothing new gets in unseen.
ladder.L4: Built the check: a step that refuses unknown packages or unreviewed plugins before they install, with a test that a made-up package name is blocked.

techniques.how: Read a skill's or plugin's files, and the events its hooks fire on, before installing. Check that its trigger is not 'every task'
techniques.laptop_signal: Built vs borrowed list: plugins from someone else's marketplace, skills installed from a registry or linked in

techniques.how: Pin plugins, MCP servers and dependencies to a version; review plugin updates and lockfile changes like dependency updates
Look up a package the agent proposes (registry page, maintainer, downloads) before it is installed
An ask rule on install commands so each install stops for a look
techniques.laptop_signal: Ask rule count (which commands it covers is not read)

vet-what-gets-in.call_evidence: They say they read a plugin's files before installing it, or that the project keeps a list of approved ones. They look up a package the agent added: that it exists, who keeps it, that it is the right name. L1: installs what is popular or whatever the agent suggests. Installing plugins is itself the floor (ruling 7). Checking them first is the practice.
vet-what-gets-in.laptop_evidence: Built vs borrowed: plugins installed from someone else's marketplace vs a folder they keep, skills installed through a registry. Not read: package installs the agent ran, pinned versions, lockfile review.
rulings: Ruling 7: 'Using them is a L1 basic thing.' Installing plugins others wrote is the floor; checking them before they get in is what this practice reads.
vet-what-gets-in.authors_note: No vocabulary term: the vocabulary names the attacks (prompt injection through installed instructions, slopsquatting) and one narrow fix filed under package hallucination ('verify packages exist before install'), but no settled name for the habit. The playbook calls it the supply chain.

ladder_short.L2: Reads a plugin or package before installing it
ladder_short.L3: Approved plugin list, pinned versions, new packages seen in review
ladder_short.L4: Built a step refusing unknown packages; a test blocks a fake

keep-outside-text-from-steering.name: Build agents so the text they read can't choose what they do
keep-outside-text-from-steering.what_you_do: When they build an agent that reads outside text (emails, web pages, tickets, user messages), they design it so that text can't pick its actions. Either the list of actions is fixed before any outside text is read, or a reader with no tools handles the outside text and passes back only results the program treats as plain data. Their own instructions sit above anything fetched.

ladder.L2: In an agent they build, reads or cleans outside text by hand before it reaches the model, or turns off the tools that can send things out while it handles outside input.
ladder.L3: Their agent's setup does it on every run: their instructions in the part the model ranks highest, outside text passed in marked as data, and tools that can send things out unavailable while untrusted text is loaded.
ladder.L4: Designed it in: a reader with no tools handles outside text and passes back only checked values, or the list of actions is fixed before any outside text is read. A set of injection attempts is run against it.

techniques.how: An agent SDK program with two roles: a reader with no tools for outside text, and an actor that only ever sees checked, typed values
techniques.laptop_signal: Files in their repos that start agents through the Agent SDK, claude -p or CI (shows they build agents, not this design)

techniques.how: Fix the list of tool calls before reading outside data (plan-then-execute)
Keep their instructions in the system prompt; pass fetched text as data, marked untrusted

keep-outside-text-from-steering.call_evidence: They have built an agent that reads outside text and can say how that text is kept from choosing its actions: what the part that reads it can and can't do. Side projects count (ruling 9).
keep-outside-text-from-steering.laptop_evidence: Files in their repos that start agents through an agent SDK show they build agents at all. Nothing on the laptop shows the design.

learn.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections (plan-then-execute)

rulings: Builder-level move: marked builds-agents, like the context discipline's builder moves (SCOPE).
Ruling 9: 'Of course side projects count towards the level'. An agent built on the side shows this as much as client work.
keep-outside-text-from-steering.authors_note: Merges: Dual LLM pattern (emerging); plan-then-execute, the security pattern and not the planning habit (single-source); instruction hierarchy (emerging), which is trained into the model and which builders use by keeping their rules in the top-ranked place.

ladder_short.L2: In an agent they build, cleans outside text by hand
ladder_short.L3: Their agent marks outside text as data on every run
ladder_short.L4: Designed it in; injection attempts are run against it

step-in-on-signals.name: Let the agent run, and step in at set points or when it signals
step-in-on-signals.what_you_do: Starts a run with what done looks like, then does other work instead of watching. Goes back at moments they chose or when the run signals it is finished, stuck or asking, and stops it when it drifts. Approving every step is the opposite of this.

ladder.L1: They sit and watch each run, approving steps and typing 'continue', or they leave it and find out late that it went wrong.
ladder.L2: By hand, they start each run with a finish line, turn to other work, go back when it finishes or asks, and stop it themselves when it drifts.
ladder.L3: Their setup tells them when to look: runs work toward a stated end, routine steps go through without asking, and a notice arrives when a run finishes, gets stuck or asks, for every run and for a teammate on the same setup.
ladder.L4: They built their own watcher that stops or flags a run that loops, runs too long or goes over a limit, without them watching, keep tuning its limits as their work changes, and a test that replays such a run shows it still catches it.

techniques.how: /goal sets an end condition the session works toward and reports against, so they look when it says met or blocked.
techniques.laptop_signal: /goal and its goal status in the session logs (scan-coverage table 2, solid)

techniques.how: Send a session to the background (/bg) or start sub-agents in the background, and come back on the finish notice.
techniques.laptop_signal: background sessions (sessionKind: bg) and sub-agents started with run_in_background

techniques.how: Let the agent watch a long process itself (Monitor, a timed wake-up) instead of the person checking on it.
techniques.laptop_signal: Monitor and ScheduleWakeup calls (92 on one laptop, one_at_a_time.py)

techniques.how: A Notification or Stop hook that pings them (desktop, phone, chat) when a run ends or asks; remote control to steer from another device.
A watcher script that reads run logs and kills or flags a run past a turn, time or cost limit, with a replayed looping run as its test (L4).

step-in-on-signals.call_evidence: Tell me about the last long task you gave an agent: what did you tell it done meant, what were you doing while it worked, and what brought you back to it?
step-in-on-signals.laptop_evidence: Reads end conditions (/goal), background sessions, Monitor and wake-up calls, and from babysitting.py how long agents wait on the person per agent hour and the long runs they stayed to watch (replied within a minute, typed nowhere else). On one laptop: about 3 minutes of waiting per agent hour, half of it plan approvals; 16 of 507 long runs watched. Can't see notifications or check-ins from another device (remote session records are in the logs but not read).
rulings: 10-27: L2 is 'scaling with discipline': several tasks run in parallel, kept on track while they run, results owned ('L2 … they scale by parallelizing tasks').
Level guide L2 line 'Steers it while it works, and stops it when it drifts' had no signal in v13; this practice is where it is now measured.

ladder_short.L2: Starts runs with a finish line, works elsewhere, and checks back
ladder_short.L3: Gets notified when a run finishes, stalls or asks for input
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a watcher that stops looping or runaway runs

step-in-on-signals.entry_rules: Counts on a real run with its finish line and what brought them back; 'I let it run' alone is could-be; watching or approving every step is L1.

parallel-work-kept-apart.name: Run several tasks at once, each in its own worktree, no more than you can review
parallel-work-kept-apart.what_you_do: Runs two or more pieces of work at the same time, each in its own session and its own copy of the code (or on files no other one touches), and knows which holds what.
