Sizes how many run at once to how much they can read back, because their reading, not the agent, is the limit.

ladder.L1: One agent at a time while they wait on it, or several in one copy of the code undoing each other's work.
ladder.L2: By hand, they open two or more sessions on separate tasks, each in its own copy or on separate files, know which holds what, and stop adding sessions when they can't keep up reading the results.
ladder.L3: Their setup starts every task in its own copy and branch, and the repo says which agent owns which folder, so the next session or a teammate starts apart without being told.
ladder.L4: They built their own program that runs agents in separate copies, merges back in order and runs the checks before anything lands, so collisions are caught without them, keep tuning it as their work changes, and a test with two agents changing the same file shows the conflict is still caught.

techniques.how: Start each task in its own worktree (claude --worktree, or git worktree add), one named session per task.
techniques.laptop_signal: worktree entries (worktree-state records: 103 in 68 sessions on one laptop)

techniques.how: Built-in fan-out: /batch or a dynamic workflow splits a change across agents in worktrees (L2 by ruling 11).
Their own agent definitions set to isolation: worktree, so separation happens by default (L3).
techniques.laptop_signal: own agent files, credited by git (scan: what they built)

techniques.how: /fork or /branch to try a second approach without disturbing the first session.
techniques.laptop_signal: forks and branches (forkedFrom, copied parent records)

techniques.how: A note in the repo saying which folder each agent owns and which shared files need coordination; separate ports and databases per copy.

parallel-work-kept-apart.call_evidence: When you last had two agents working at once, where did each one's changes live, and how many do you run before you can't keep up reading what they hand back?
parallel-work-kept-apart.laptop_evidence: Reads agents at once, worktree entries, forks, workflow runs and one-agent stretches (one_at_a_time.py). On one laptop: two or more agents at once 77% of busy time, 103 worktree entries, 116 workflow calls. Can't tell a fork of the same session from two unrelated tasks, nor whether parallel sessions touched the same files.
rulings: 10-20 (parallel sessions and side work in sub-agents): 'That's L2 thing that carries over in L3'.
Ruling 11: dynamic workflows / ultracode 'it's an L2 thing'.
10-27: 'L2 … they scale by parallelizing tasks'.
parallel-work-kept-apart.authors_note: No vocabulary term: the field names this only through its tools (worktrees, parallel sessions). Sending exploration to a sub-agent is the context discipline's sub-agent practice.

ladder_short.L2: Runs separate sessions by hand, no more than they can read
ladder_short.L3: Sets up each task to start in its own worktree and branch
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that merges parallel work and catches conflicts

parallel-work-kept-apart.entry_rules: Two pieces of work in their own sessions is L2 and carries into L3 (10-20); naming review as the bottleneck counts only when they size the parallel work to it.

lead-a-team-of-agents.name: Split one job across agents: who does what, and how it comes back
lead-a-team-of-agents.what_you_do: Acts as team lead for one job: splits it across two or more agents, says who does which part and what each must hand back, then reads and merges what comes back before going on. Switching between unrelated sessions is parallel work, not this; one agent running a long command is not this either.

ladder.L1: Agents on one job, or helpers the agent starts on its own, work with no split they designed, and the pieces come back overlapping or not fitting.
ladder.L2: For one job, they split the work by hand across agents, give each a part and say what to hand back, then read and merge the results; running a dynamic workflow that spreads one job over many agents, then reading it back and rerunning it, counts here (ruling 11).
ladder.L3: The split lives in their setup: role definitions, a command of theirs (for example plan, build, review) or a saved workflow script runs the same team the same way on the next job or for a teammate.
ladder.L4: They built their own coordinator that starts the agents, passes work and results between them and decides what comes next without them stitching the pieces, keep tuning it as their jobs change, and evals on past jobs show its output still holds.

techniques.how: Sub-agents each given one part of the job with a brief that says what to hand back.
techniques.laptop_signal: sub-agents started, their type, model and what each was sent to do; who split the work, the agent or the person (v_who_split_the_work)

techniques.how: Agent teams: a lead creates tasks, teammates take parts and message each other.
techniques.laptop_signal: teams, task tools and messages between sessions (counted; what they say is never read)

techniques.how: Dynamic workflows (ultracode): the tool writes the orchestration script; they scope it, read it back and rerun it (L2 by ruling 11).
techniques.laptop_signal: Workflow tool calls (runs only; the agents and phases inside a run are not read)

techniques.how: Their own agent files and a command or skill that runs plan, build and review the same way each time (L3).
techniques.laptop_signal: own agents, commands and skills, credited by git

techniques.how: Their own coordinator on an agent SDK or headless runs that starts agents and routes results, with evals on past jobs (L4); installing a ready-made orchestration framework alone is L1.

lead-a-team-of-agents.call_evidence: Tell me about one job you split across several agents: who did which part, what did each hand back, and how did you put it together and check it?
lead-a-team-of-agents.laptop_evidence: Reads sub-agents (type, model, task), teams, messages between sessions, workflow runs, own agents and commands credited by git, and sub-agents the agent chose against those the person asked for (on one laptop over 90 days: 2,020 chosen by the agent, 78 asked for by command). Can't read inside a workflow run, sub-agents started by sub-agents, or what sessions say to each other, so it can't yet tell one job split from many unrelated sub-agents.
rulings: 10-07: 'Imagine you're a team lead and you orchestrate your team for an effort, who does what and how? It at least implies that the person has multiple agents being coordinated effectively.' Several unrelated sessions switched between = not it; one agent running a multi-step command = not it.
Ruling 11: dynamic workflows / ultracode 'it's an L2 thing'; 'Building your own orchestration program that starts agents is still Level 4.'
10-09: 'There's also a lot of other features that indicate multi-agent orchestration: branching, use of /subtask (subagents) and /goal… Claude is evolving, maybe our substrate should as well.'
lead-a-team-of-agents.authors_note: No vocabulary term: the field names the shape 'orchestrator-worker' inside sub-agent architectures (a context move), but has no entry for the person's practice of leading the split.

ladder_short.L2: Splits one job across agents, or runs a dynamic workflow
ladder_short.L3: Saves roles, a command or a workflow script that reruns the team
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a coordinator that runs the agents without them

lead-a-team-of-agents.entry_rules: One job, two or more agents, their design of who does what and how it comes back (10-07); helpers the agent started on its own get no credit; built-in workflows are L2, their own program L4 (ruling 11).

fresh-run-per-task.name: Work through a long list with a fresh run per item, keeping progress in files
fresh-run-per-task.what_you_do: Gives each item of a long list (every ticket, every file, a backlog) its own fresh agent run with the same instructions, and keeps progress in a file and in version history instead of in the session. No session fills up and degrades, and a crash or a stop costs one item, not the whole job.

ladder.L1: A long list runs in one session that gets worse as it fills, and a crash or a stop loses the progress.
ladder.L2: By hand, they start a fresh session per item from a progress file updated after each one, or run the tool's built-in loop or workflow over the list.
ladder.L3: The loop lives in their repo: saved instructions, a progress file and a command of theirs that picks the next unfinished item, so any run or a teammate carries on where the last one stopped.
ladder.L4: They built their own runner that starts fresh runs through the list until the checks pass, resumes from the progress file after a crash and stops at a limit, all without them, keep tuning it as their lists change, and a test that kills a run midway shows it picks up where it stopped.

techniques.how: A shell loop that feeds the same prompt file to a fresh headless run until the list is done (known as the Ralph loop); their own script, so L4 once it has a resume test.
techniques.laptop_signal: headless runs by who started them, and batches of headless runs in one project (scan: headless_by_starter, headless_batches)

techniques.how: A progress file in the repo that each run reads first and updates last.
techniques.laptop_signal: new sessions that open by reading a file an earlier session wrote (starts_from_zero.py)

techniques.how: Headless runs (claude -p) with --max-turns and --max-budget-usd so one stuck item can't eat the night.
techniques.laptop_signal: bounded headless calls (scan: headless_bounded_calls)

techniques.how: A dynamic workflow with one agent per item (L2 by ruling 11); /loop or the ralph-wiggum plugin repeat inside one window, so they do not give a fresh start per item.

fresh-run-per-task.call_evidence: Tell me about the last time an agent went through a long list of items: where was it kept what was done, and what happened when a run failed or stopped halfway?
fresh-run-per-task.laptop_evidence: Reads headless runs by who started them, batches of runs in one project, runs with limits set, /loop timers, and new sessions that open on a file an earlier session wrote. Can't yet tell one fresh run per list item from unrelated runs, or whether a run resumed after a crash (today only 'automated runs edited tooling' is read).
rulings: Ruling 11: dynamic workflows / ultracode 'it's an L2 thing'; recorded meaning: 'Building your own orchestration program that starts agents is still Level 4.' A built-in loop is L2; their own loop script is L4.
L4 needs evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces the 10-09/10-13 'evals the agent can't edit').
fresh-run-per-task.authors_note: Merges: the Ralph loop, walking a whole set on its own, and a run that picks up after a crash from the progress file.

ladder_short.L2: Starts a fresh session per item by hand, from a progress file
ladder_short.L3: Keeps the loop in the repo, so anyone resumes where it stopped
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a runner that resumes from the progress file

fresh-run-per-task.entry_rules: Needs a list the system holds and progress kept outside the session; 'twenty agents at once' is parallel work, not this (v13 loop-21 wording watch).

runs-start-without-you.name: Have agent runs start from a schedule or an event, not from your typing
runs-start-without-you.what_you_do: Lets a schedule or an event (a new ticket, a pull request, a failing build) start the agent with saved instructions, and the result waits as a draft for a person to decide on. Automates only what already works by hand on a few real tasks, with each correction moved into the saved instructions first.

ladder.L1: Every run starts because they typed it, so routine jobs wait for them.
ladder.L2: By hand, they leave one long task running in the background or on a timer, walk away, and review what it left when they come back.
ladder.L3: Set up once, it runs again and again: a schedule, a build step or a ticket label starts the agent with saved instructions and limits, nobody types, and they or a teammate read the result later.
ladder.L4: They built their own program that listens for events and starts runs limited in what each may do and spend, acts on what comes back with nobody starting them, keep tuning it as their routine jobs change, and known cases rerun after each change show the results still hold.

techniques.how: /schedule or a desktop scheduled task runs a saved prompt on a cadence.
techniques.laptop_signal: scheduled task fires in the logs (scheduled_task_fire; fired in 10 sessions on one laptop)

techniques.how: A cron, launchd or systemd timer that starts a headless agent run with a fixed prompt, tool list and turn cap.
An agent step in the build pipeline that runs on pull requests or issues (for example the Claude Code GitHub action).
techniques.laptop_signal: CI agent in the repo's workflow files (scan: has_ci_agent)

techniques.how: Their own listener (webhook, ticket board) on an agent SDK that starts runs with their own tools and permission rules (L4).

runs-start-without-you.call_evidence: Which agent runs start without you typing anything: what starts them, what instructions do they get, where does the result land, and who built it?
runs-start-without-you.laptop_evidence: Reads scheduled task fires, OS jobs that start an agent, a CI agent in the repo, scripts that start agents (credited by git) and runs left alone that ended in kept work. On one laptop: scheduled tasks fired in 10 sessions, no OS job starts an agent, 28 runs left alone of which 29% ended in a commit. Runs on other machines or in a client's pipeline are out of sight.
rulings: 10-12 (a team cron job he can explain): 'The fact that "we have" as a team and he's aware of it, already should activate the atom'; the build leg (L4) still needs that they built it.
Ruling 2: 'Setting up claude's behavior via hooks tooling or anything else, is mostly L4'.
L4 needs evals, period: whether the agent can edit them is not part of the bar (11-02, replaces the 10-09/10-13 'evals the agent can't edit').

practice_card.title: Make it work by hand on a few real tickets before automating
practice_card.text: Sit with the agent through a handful of real tickets, note each correction and move it into the instructions, keep a few evals with known outputs, and only when results are reliably acceptable put it in CI, a scheduled job or a bot. Keep a human gate on merge. Start automation with preparation tasks that produce a draft (triage, checklists, branch setup).

runs-start-without-you.authors_note: Merges: scheduled agents, triggered agents, agents in the build pipeline, and something they built that acts on its own when it sees a condition. No vocabulary term: the field's list has no entry for agents that start themselves.

ladder_short.L2: Starts a long task, walks away, and reviews it later
ladder_short.L3: Sets a schedule or event to start runs from saved instructions
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a program that starts limited runs on events

runs-start-without-you.entry_rules: A team job they can explain what and how counts at L3 (10-12); L4 needs they built it, and the L4 laptop check proves the build only, the known-case rerun is asked on the call.

model-and-budget-per-step.name: Match the model and the spend to each step, and judge runs by what they leave
model-and-budget-per-step.what_you_do: Chooses which model does which step for a reason: a strong one to plan or review, a cheaper or faster one to search or make routine edits. Puts a turn or cost limit on runs nobody watches, and judges a run by what it left, not by how much it used.

ladder.L1: One model for everything, no limit on unwatched runs, and no idea what a run cost or left behind.
ladder.L2: By hand, they switch model when the kind of step changes and can say why, look at what runs cost and did, and stop a run that burns money for little.
ladder.L3: Their setup chooses: their own agent roles name the model for each, a default pairs a planning model with a building one, and unattended runs carry a turn or cost limit, so every run and teammate gets it without choosing.
ladder.L4: They built their own program that picks the model per step, stops any run over its limit and records cost against what each run left, without them watching, keep tuning the choices as their work changes, and a test with an over-limit run shows it still gets stopped.

techniques.how: /model or effort level changed mid-session when the step changes; opusplan to plan on one model and build on another.
A model named in their own agent definitions or on each sub-agent call (cheap to search, strong to review); L3 when it is in their own definitions.
techniques.laptop_signal: sub-agent calls with a model set, and sub-agents by model (scan: subagent_calls_with_model)

techniques.how: --max-turns and --max-budget-usd on headless runs; /cost, /usage or /stats to see what a session spent.
A usage export or telemetry that sets cost per run against what the run kept (a usage view, not a leaderboard).
techniques.laptop_signal: cost per session (read and summed for one number only; no check uses it)

model-and-budget-per-step.call_evidence: Which model does which kind of step in your work, and why? Tell me about a run you stopped or changed because of what it cost.
model-and-budget-per-step.laptop_evidence: Reads models per session, model switches, sub-agent calls with a model set, runs with turn or spend limits, and summed cost. Effort level, thinking budget and per-run budget records are in the logs but not read, and no check yet compares cost with kept work.
rulings: No ruling on its level: the level guide lists model routing as pending ('its level was never ruled').
model-and-budget-per-step.authors_note: Merges model routing, circuit breakers on runaway runs, and 'judge outcomes, not token counts' (the vocabulary's fixes for token maxxing). No vocabulary term: 'model routing' is a playbook word, not in the field's list.

ladder_short.L2: Switches model by hand when the step changes and checks cost
ladder_short.L3: Sets the model per agent role and limits on unattended runs
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests tooling that picks models and enforces limits

model-and-budget-per-step.short_name: Set model and budget per step
model-and-budget-per-step.entry_rules: A model tied to a kind of step, with a reason; switching vendor for price or 'the bigger one is better' is not this; its level was never ruled, so this ladder needs his yes.

coordinate-live-agents.name: Let agents that run at the same time talk to each other and hand work back
coordinate-live-agents.what_you_do: When several agents work on related parts of one effort at the same time, they don't work blind to each other: one can tell another what it found, ask it for something, or hand a piece of work back, and the person reads where things stand instead of relaying every finding between sessions themselves. This is about agents already running in parallel exchanging work while they run; splitting one job into roles up front is "lead a team of agents", and unrelated sessions side by side are parallel work.

ladder.L1: Several sessions run on related work, but none knows what the others found; the person copies results between them, or two collide.
ladder.L2: They relay between sessions by hand on purpose, telling one session what another found, or forking a session to carry its context, and check on each before they cross.
ladder.L3: Their setup lets live agents message each other and hand work back (named sessions or an agent team with a lead), so findings and requests travel between agents and the person reads one status, not every session.
ladder.L4: They built their own coordination layer (a registry of live sessions, routing of messages and handoffs) that runs without them, keep tuning it as their work changes, and a test shows a message and a handed-back piece of work arrive where they should.

techniques.how: Agent teams: a lead and teammates that take tasks and message each other.
techniques.laptop_signal: teams, teammates, task tools and messages between sessions (counted; contents never read)

techniques.how: Sending a message from one live session to another, and forking a session to carry its context into a new one.
techniques.laptop_signal: messages to other sessions (counted), forked sessions

techniques.how: Their own session registry and message routing, with a test that a handoff arrives (L4).

coordinate-live-agents.call_evidence: When you have several sessions going on related work, how does one learn what another found? Walk me through the last time two agents passed work between them.
coordinate-live-agents.laptop_evidence: Claude Code records messages sent between sessions, teams, teammates and tasks: counted, never read. Not yet a trusted check, so it can't set a level; it's shown and asked on the call.
rulings: 11-06: his call: "sessions that talk to each other should be a multi-agent orchestration practice". 10-09: "a lot of other features indicate multi-agent orchestration: branching, use of /subtask (subagents)".

ladder_short.L2: Relays findings between sessions by hand, on purpose
ladder_short.L3: Lets live agents message each other and hand work back
ladder_short.L4: Builds, tunes and tests a layer that routes work between agents

context-rot.meaning: A model's accuracy and recall degrade as the number of tokens in its context grows, so more context is not automatically better. Anthropic: 'As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot'.
context-rot.who: Hacker News user Workaccount2 (comment of 2025-06-18; Simon Willison replied 'I think you just coined context rot'). Measured by Chroma (Kelly Hong, Anton Troynikov, Jeff Huber, 2025-07-14, 18 models), whose report uses the term only in its title. Defined in Anthropic's docs and engineering post (2025-09-29).

page.label: Context rot
page.text: The more tokens in the context, the worse the model recalls and reasons. More context is not automatically better.
page.named_by: A Hacker News comment (June 2025), measured by Chroma, defined by Anthropic

lost-in-the-middle.meaning: Language model performance is often highest when the relevant information sits at the beginning or end of the input. It degrades significantly when that information sits in the middle of a long context, even for explicitly long-context models.
lost-in-the-middle.who: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang (TACL 2023). The labels U-shaped, primacy and recency come from later writers. This is a different measured effect from context rot: Chroma found no position effect in its own setup.
fixed_by: placing critical information at the start or end of the prompt

page.label: Lost in the middle
page.text: Facts at the start or end of a long input get used; facts in the middle get missed.

context-poisoning.grade_note: one researcher and the checker rate it standard
context-poisoning.meaning: A hallucination or other error gets into the context. The model refers back to it again and again, and it keeps steering the model.
context-poisoning.who: Google DeepMind's Gemini 2.5 team, in the Gemini Plays Pokemon section of the technical report (arXiv 2507.06261). Drew Breunig generalised it as a failure mode and popularised it (2025-06-22). Adopted by LangChain, Simon Willison and OpenAI's Agents SDK cookbook. Not the same as trajectory poisoning.
fixed_by: compaction (only with a clean summary; a bad fact in a summary keeps poisoning)

page.label: Context poisoning
page.text: A wrong fact or hallucination gets into the context, and the model keeps building on it.

context-distraction.meaning: A context grows so long that the model over-focuses on the context and neglects what it learned during training.
context-distraction.who: Drew Breunig (2025-06-22). LangChain ('When the context overwhelms the training') and Willison adopted it, citing him. Not the same as Chroma's 'distractors'.

page.label: Context distraction
page.text: The context grows so long that the model leans on it and neglects what it learned in training.

context-confusion.meaning: The model uses superfluous content in the context to generate a low-quality response. Breunig's main evidence is too many tool definitions: the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, and a GeoEngine study where a quantized Llama 3.1 8b failed with 46 tools and succeeded with 19. It does not mean the agent is confused about which task or project it is on.
context-confusion.who: Drew Breunig, 'How Long Contexts Fail' (2025-06-22), restated in 'How to Fix Your Context' (2025-06-26). Lance Martin/LangChain, Simon Willison, O'Reilly Radar and Redis repeat it and credit him. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Chroma and academic papers do not use it.

page.label: Context confusion
page.text: Extra content, most often too many tool definitions, drags the answer down.

context-clash.meaning: New information and tools added to the context conflict with information already in it.
context-clash.who: Drew Breunig (2025-06-22). He builds it on Laban et al. (arXiv 2505.06120), who found an average 39% drop when prompts are split across turns. LangChain lists it and Willison quotes it.
fixed_by: single-threaded agents with shared full traces (Cognition)

page.label: Context clash
page.text: New information conflicts with what is already in the context.

lost-in-conversation.meaning: When an LLM takes a wrong turn in a multi-turn conversation, it gets lost and does not recover. It makes assumptions early and attempts final answers too soon, then over-relies on them. The study measured an average 39% drop versus single-turn prompts.
lost-in-conversation.who: Philippe Laban, Hiroaki Hayashi, Yingbo Zhou, Jennifer Neville, 'LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation' (2025-05-09). 'Lost in conversation' is the name of the code repository.
also_called: LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
fixed_by: consolidating requirements into a fresh single-turn prompt

page.label: Lost in conversation
page.text: One wrong turn early in a multi-turn session and the model rarely recovers. The study measured a 39% average drop versus one complete prompt.

context-pollution.meaning: Irrelevant or stale content builds up in the context window, such as unrelated tasks or failed approaches, and degrades the model's output.
context-pollution.who: No known coiner. Anthropic uses it descriptively without defining it: in its engineering post (2025-09-29) and in the Claude Code docs ('Context is polluted with failed approaches'). Per the checker, Phil Schmid (Dec 2025) and Liip (Mar 2026) define it independently.

page.label: Context pollution
page.text: Irrelevant or stale content, such as failed attempts and unrelated tasks, piles up and degrades the output.
page.named_by: No single author; used by Anthropic

attention-budget.meaning: LLMs have an attention budget that they draw on when parsing large volumes of context, and every new token depletes it by some amount. Anthropic grounds the idea in the transformer's n-squared pairwise relationships being stretched thin.
attention-budget.who: Anthropic Applied AI team (Prithvi Rajasekaran, Ethan Dixon, Carly Ryan, Jeremy Hadfield), 2025-09-29.

page.label: Attention budget
page.text: The model has a limited budget of attention, and every token spends some of it.

attention-dilution.meaning: As context grows, attention is spread over more tokens, which starves the content tokens that matter. One paper defines it as 'the starvation of content tokens in the attention distribution'.
attention-dilution.who: Unknown. The earliest uses found are in Shangding Gu, 'Long Context, Less Focus' (arXiv 2602.15028, 2026-02-16), and Pei et al., FocuSFT (arXiv 2605.09932, 2026-05-11). The first is about inference and the second about training, so the two papers use the term somewhat differently.

real-context-size.term: real context size (claimed versus effective context length)
real-context-size.meaning: Effective context length is the longest input at which a model still performs above a quality threshold. It is often far below the context length the model claims or was trained on: RULER tested 17 models and found only half held up at 32K.
real-context-size.who: No single coiner. RULER (Hsieh et al., NVIDIA, 2024-04-09) popularised measuring claimed against effective length, and An et al. (2024-10-24) use 'effective context length' in their title.

context-anxiety.meaning: A model that knows the size of its own context window takes shortcuts or wraps tasks up early because it believes it is near the end of the window, even when plenty of room is left.
context-anxiety.who: Cognition (the Devin team), in 'Rebuilding Devin for Claude Sonnet 4.5' (2025-09-29). Adopted by Inkeep (2025-10-03) and in Anthropic's harness post (2026-03-24). A 2026 ICML paper (arXiv 2607.21616) calls it 'informally known as context anxiety'.
fixed_by: enable the 1M-token window but cap usage at 200k (Cognition)
reminders at the start and end of the prompt
tell the model its context will be compacted and not to stop early

page.label: Context anxiety
page.text: A model that knows its window size rushes or wraps up early, believing it is near the end when it isn't.

dumb-zone.meaning: The stretch of a filled-up context window where a coding agent's decisions get noticeably worse. In that stretch it starts doing increasingly stupid things, such as deleting your .env file. The low-utilisation counterpart is the smart zone.
dumb-zone.who: Attributed to Dex Horthy (HumanLayer), who introduced it jokingly in his AI Engineer Code 2025 talk 'No Vibes Allowed'. No fetched source states that he coined it. He credits Geoff Huntley for the idea that the more of the window you use, the worse the outcomes.
fixed_by: keep context utilisation low (Horthy's ~40% heuristic, a feel not a measured constant)

page.label: Dumb zone
page.text: Past a certain fill level, the agent's decisions get noticeably worse.

trajectory-poisoning.meaning: The agent falls into a pattern of doing things you do not want. After repeated mistakes, the model computes that the most probable next message is another mistake. Replies such as 'You're completely right!' are a symptom.
trajectory-poisoning.who: Gergely Orosz's write-up of Dex Horthy (2026-07-15). The wording may be Orosz's.

summary-drift.meaning: When history is compressed into a summary, facts get reinterpreted or altered, so errors can compound across repeated summarisation.
summary-drift.who: Unknown. The exact phrase appears in OpenAI's Agents SDK cookbook (undated). Factory Research (2025-12-16) calls the same effect 'silent drift'.

context-collapse.meaning: When an LLM repeatedly rewrites an accumulated context, details erode over time and the context degrades into shorter, less informative summaries.
context-collapse.who: Qizheng Zhang et al., 'Agentic Context Engineering' (arXiv 2510.04618, 2025-10-06; ICLR 2026). Unrelated to 'model collapse'.
also_called: brevity bias (sibling term from the same paper)

page.label: Context collapse
page.text: Summarising a context again and again erodes the details until little useful is left.

lobotomization.meaning: After auto-compaction, a coding agent loses track of which repo it is in, forgets constraints you set and drops skills it had invoked, so session quality falls immediately.
lobotomization.who: Unknown; community slang. Ian L. Paterson (2026-03-25, updated 2026-08-15) reports 'The community calls this lobotomization'. The behaviour is documented in Claude Code issue #24460 (2026-02-09): /compact summarises CLAUDE.md rules along with the conversation, and they may be lost. The issue was closed as not planned.

instruction-drift.meaning: A model follows its initial instructions less and less as a conversation or session grows, even though the instructions are still in context. Li et al. report significant drift within eight rounds and tie it to attention decay. Bui's name, instruction fade-out, describes the model progressively deprioritising initial instructions as history grows.
instruction-drift.who: 'Instruction drift': Kenneth Li, Tianle Liu, Naomi Bashkansky, David Bau, Fernanda Viegas, Hanspeter Pfister, Martin Wattenberg (arXiv 2402.10962, 2024-02-13; COLM 2024; first framed as 'persona drift'). 'Instruction fade-out': Nghi D. Q. Bui's OPENDEV paper (arXiv 2603.05344, 2026-03-05), defined by agentpatterns.ai. 'Context drift': practitioner usage with no coiner, also used for state lost between sessions. No settled name exists.

goal-drift.meaning: An agent's tendency to deviate from its original objective over time. Arike et al. find that it correlates with growing susceptibility to pattern-matching as context length grows.
goal-drift.who: Rauno Arike, Elizabeth Donoway, Henning Bartsch, Marius Hobbhahn (arXiv 2505.02709, 2025-05-05; AIES 2025). Follow-ups by other authors reuse the term (arXiv 2603.03258, 2603.03456).

page.label: Goal drift
page.text: Over a long run, the agent wanders away from its original objective.

agent-drift.meaning: The progressive degradation of agent behavior, decision quality and inter-agent coherence over extended interaction sequences.
agent-drift.who: Abhishek Rath (independent researcher), arXiv 2601.04170, 2026-01-07. The results come from simulation and the researchers read only the abstract.

instruction-induction-conflict.meaning: In a long conversation, the user's instruction can compete with the pattern set by earlier assistant turns. When it does, the model switches from following the instruction to continuing the pattern.
instruction-induction-conflict.who: Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller (arXiv 2605.20382, 2026-05-19; poster at the COLM 2026 Sci-FM workshop).
fixed_by: chain-of-thought (helps but does not remove it)

context-inertia.meaning: The model commits to a hypothesis, subtask or goal in its context and keeps pursuing it after the evidence says to stop or change course.
context-inertia.who: Drew Breunig, 2026-10-14. He says compaction alone does not fix it. Nobody checked whether the works he cites use the term themselves.

kitchen-sink-session.meaning: You start with one task, ask something unrelated, then return to the first task. The context is left full of irrelevant information.
kitchen-sink-session.who: Anthropic, in the Claude Code best-practices docs, next to its sibling anti-patterns 'Correcting over and over' and 'The infinite exploration'.

page.label: Kitchen sink session
page.text: One session for unrelated tasks, so each task's leftovers crowd the next.

context-engineering.meaning: The set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference (Anthropic). Karpathy calls it 'the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step'.
context-engineering.who: Contested; no single coiner. The Pragmatic Engineer asserts Dex Horthy coined it. Horthy himself recalls posting 12-Factor Agents around 2025-04-03 and calls Jeff Huber a 'secret co-creator'; he does not claim coinage. Earliest dated uses verified: Walden Yan/Cognition 2025-06-12, Tobi Lütke 2025-06-19, Harrison Chase 2025-06-23, Andrej Karpathy 2025-06-25.

page.label: Context engineering
page.text: The umbrella: choose and maintain the right tokens in the window for each step.

smallest-set-of-high-signal-tokens.meaning: Find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the likelihood of your desired outcome. Minimal does not mean short.
smallest-set-of-high-signal-tokens.who: Anthropic Applied AI team (Rajasekaran, Dixon, Ryan, Hadfield), 2025-09-29.
also_called: not too little, not too much (Böckeler)

progressive-disclosure.meaning: The core design principle of Agent Skills: load information only as needed, in levels. The skill's metadata sits in the system prompt, the SKILL.md body loads when relevant, and linked files load only for specific scenarios. Anthropic applies the same principle to tool definitions.
progressive-disclosure.who: Borrowed from HCI/UX: a 2006 Nielsen Norman Group article calls it over 30 years old and names no originator. Anthropic applied it to agents (Barry Zhang, Keith Lazuka, Mahesh Murag) in the Agent Skills post, 2025-10-16.

page.label: Progressive disclosure
page.text: Keep a short version always loaded and open the detail only when it is needed. The design idea behind Agent Skills.
page.named_by: From UX design; Anthropic for agents

just-in-time-context-retrieval.meaning: Agents keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths, stored queries and web links. They load the data into context at runtime with tools, instead of pre-loading everything.
just-in-time-context-retrieval.who: Anthropic Applied AI team (2025-09-29). Cursor's Jediah Katz named the same pattern 'dynamic context discovery' (2026-01-06).

page.label: Just-in-time retrieval
page.text: Keep pointers (file paths, queries, links) and load the content at the moment it is needed.

compaction.meaning: When a conversation nears the context window limit, summarize its contents and start a new context window with the summary. It is lossy.
compaction.who: Originator unknown. Defined by Anthropic's Applied AI team (2025-09-29), which calls it 'the first lever in context engineering'. Shipped by Claude Code, the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs, Google ADK and Amp. Breunig names the underlying move 'context summarization' (2025-06-26). Manus uses 'compaction' for something different: swapping stale tool results for file pointers.

page.label: Compaction
page.text: Summarise the conversation near the limit and continue in a fresh window from the summary.

intentional-compaction.meaning: As the context starts to fill, pause and have the agent distil the work so far into a reviewable structured artifact, such as progress.md, that keeps the exact files and line numbers that matter. Then start a fresh agent from it. Do this often, keeping utilisation around 40-60%.
intentional-compaction.who: Dex Horthy (HumanLayer), blog post 'Advanced context engineering' (2025-08-29) and AI Engineer Code 2025 talk.

page.label: Intentional compaction
page.text: Before the window fills, have the agent write the work so far into a file you can review, then continue from that.

tool-result-clearing.meaning: Automatically clearing stale tool calls and results from the context window when approaching token limits, while keeping the flow of the conversation. Clearing invalidates the cached prompt prefix.
tool-result-clearing.who: Anthropic. The Effective Context Engineering post (2025-09-29) calls it 'one of the safest lightest touch forms of compaction'; the API feature is called context editing.

structured-note-taking.meaning: The agent regularly writes notes to memory stored outside the context window, and pulls them back into the window later.

page.label: Structured note-taking
page.text: The agent writes notes outside the window and reads them back later.

sub-agent-architectures.meaning: Specialized sub-agents handle focused tasks in clean, isolated context windows and return a condensed summary of their work, often 1,000-2,000 tokens. Breunig's 'context quarantine' is the same move: isolating contexts in their own dedicated threads.
sub-agent-architectures.who: Named by Anthropic (multi-agent research system 2025-06-13; Effective Context Engineering 2025-09-29). Drew Breunig calls it 'context quarantine' (2025-06-26) and LangChain calls it 'isolate'. Counter-position: Cognition's 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (2025-06-12).

page.label: Sub-agents (context isolation)
page.text: Hand a focused task to a sub-agent with its own clean window; only a short summary comes back.

write-select-compress-isolate.meaning: Four buckets of context-engineering strategy: write context outside the window, select it into the window, compress it to the tokens required, and isolate it by splitting it up.
write-select-compress-isolate.who: Lance Martin and the LangChain team (Martin's blog 2025-06-23; LangChain blog 2025-07-02). It builds on Karpathy's OS analogy and Breunig's failure modes.

page.label: Write, select, compress, isolate
page.text: Four groups of moves: write context outside the window, select what goes in, compress it, split it up.

rag.meaning: Selectively adding relevant information to help the LLM generate a better response (Breunig's framing). Lewis et al. define RAG as models that combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for generation.
rag.who: Patrick Lewis et al. (Facebook AI Research, UCL, NYU), arXiv 2005.11401, 2020-05-22. Breunig lists it first of his six context fixes (2025-06-26).

page.label: RAG
page.text: Fetch only the relevant information into the context instead of loading everything.

tool-loadout.meaning: The act of selecting only relevant tool definitions to add to your context.
tool-loadout.who: Drew Breunig (2025-06-26), borrowing 'loadout' from gaming. Anthropic's Tool Search Tool is a productised version but never uses the word.

page.label: Tool loadout
page.text: Load only the tool definitions this task needs.

context-pruning.meaning: The act of removing irrelevant or otherwise unneeded information from the context. Breunig's pruning removes content by relevance; OpenAI's trimming removes it by age, keeping the last N turns.
context-pruning.who: Drew Breunig named it (2025-06-26). He traces the idea to pre-ChatGPT NLP and cites Provence as a pruning tool.

page.label: Context pruning
page.text: Remove what the task no longer needs.

context-offloading.meaning: Storing information outside the LLM's context, usually through a tool that stores and manages the data. Manus treats the file system as the ultimate context: unlimited, persistent and directly operable. That makes compression restorable, for example by dropping a page's content but keeping its URL.
context-offloading.who: 'Context offloading' is Drew Breunig's phrase (2025-06-26). 'File system as context' is Yichao 'Peak' Ji's (Manus, 2025-07-18), and LangChain credits Manus as one of the first to discuss it publicly. LangChain, Cursor, Google ADK, OpenAI and Anthropic describe the same move.

page.label: Context offloading
page.text: Store information outside the context, such as in files or notes, and read it back when needed.

design-around-the-kv-cache.meaning: The KV-cache hit rate is the single most important metric for a production-stage agent. So keep the prompt prefix stable, make the context append-only, and mark cache breakpoints explicitly.
design-around-the-kv-cache.who: Yichao 'Peak' Ji (Manus), 2025-07-18. Google ADK echoes it as 'stable prefixes'.
fixes: latency and token cost (cached input about 10x cheaper, per Manus)

mask-don-t-remove.meaning: Do not add or remove tools in the middle of an iteration. Instead, mask the token logits during decoding to prevent or force the selection of certain actions.
mask-don-t-remove.who: Yichao 'Peak' Ji (Manus), 2025-07-18. This is the opposite choice to tool loadout and deferred tool loading.
fixes: model confusion over missing tool definitions

recitation.meaning: By constantly rewriting a todo list, the agent recites its objectives into the end of the context, a deliberate way to pull attention toward the global plan.
recitation.who: Yichao 'Peak' Ji (Manus), 2025-07-18. LangChain reuses the phrase (2025-11-21). Manus later dropped todo.md because about a third of all actions went into updating it.

page.label: Recitation
page.text: Keep rewriting a `todo.md` so the plan stays at the end of the context, where attention is strongest.

keep-the-wrong-stuff-in.meaning: Leave wrong turns in the context: failed actions, errors, stack traces. Erasing failure removes the evidence, and without evidence the model cannot adapt.
keep-the-wrong-stuff-in.who: Yichao 'Peak' Ji (Manus), 2025-07-18. Contested by Anthropic's advice to /clear after two failed corrections, and by the context-poisoning literature.

context-reset.meaning: Clear the context window entirely and start a fresh agent, with a structured handoff that carries over the previous agent's state and next steps. Amp's handoff does the same: instead of summarizing the old thread, it extracts what matters for the next task into a new one.
context-reset.who: 'Context reset': Anthropic (Prithvi Rajasekaran, Anthropic Labs, 2026-03-24). 'Handoff': Amp (Sourcegraph, 2025-10-23). Amp reversed course in 2026-05 ('handoff is out. Compaction is in').

page.label: Context reset (handoff)
page.text: Clear the window entirely and start a fresh agent, with a written handoff of state and next steps.

context-folding.meaning: The agent branches into a sub-trajectory to handle a subtask. When the subtask is done, it folds the branch: the intermediate steps collapse and only a concise summary of the outcome is kept. The method requires training the model with RL (FoldGRPO).
context-folding.who: Weiwei Sun, Miao Lu, Zhan Ling, Kang Liu, Xuesong Yao, Yiming Yang, Jiecao Chen (arXiv 2510.11967, 2025-10-13).

recursive-language-models.meaning: A general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment. The LLM examines and decomposes the prompt through code and recursively calls itself over snippets of it.
recursive-language-models.who: Alex L. Zhang, Tim Kraska, Omar Khattab (MIT), arXiv 2512.24601, 2025-12-31.
also_called: context as a variable in a REPL
fixes: prompts larger than the context window

sleep-time-compute.meaning: Letting models think offline about contexts before queries arrive: they anticipate likely questions and precompute useful information, which cuts work at test time.
sleep-time-compute.who: Kevin Lin, Charlie Snell, Yu Wang, Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez (arXiv 2504.13171, 2025-04-17).

virtual-context-management.meaning: A technique modelled on the hierarchical memory of traditional operating systems. It gives an LLM the appearance of a larger context by moving data between fast and slow memory tiers.
virtual-context-management.who: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, Vivian Fang, Shishir G. Patil, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez (arXiv 2310.08560, 2023-10-12).

anchored-iterative-summarization.meaning: Keep a structured, persistent summary with explicit sections: session intent, file modifications, decisions, next steps. When compression triggers, summarize only the newly truncated span and merge it into the existing summary.
anchored-iterative-summarization.who: Factory Research (Factory.ai), 2025-12-16. The benchmark is vendor-run and has not been independently replicated.

agentic-context-engineering.meaning: Treat contexts as evolving playbooks that accumulate, refine and organize strategies through a cycle of generation, reflection and curation, updated with structured incremental edits.
agentic-context-engineering.who: Qizheng Zhang et al. (13 authors, including James Zou and Kunle Olukotun), arXiv 2510.04618, 2025-10-06; ICLR 2026. The paper uses 'agentic context engineering' in a narrower sense than the general discipline.

tool-search-tool.meaning: A search tool that lets Claude discover tools on demand. Tools marked defer_loading: true are not loaded into context at the start. In Anthropic's example, upfront usage fell from about 77K to about 8.7K tokens.
tool-search-tool.who: Anthropic, 'Advanced tool use' (Bin Wu with contributors), 2025-11-24.

page.label: Tool search
page.text: Let the agent search for tools on demand instead of loading them all up front.

programmatic-tool-calling.meaning: Claude orchestrates tools through code rather than through individual API round-trips. Intermediate tool results are processed in the execution environment instead of entering the context window.
programmatic-tool-calling.who: Anthropic. 'Code execution with MCP' (Adam Jones, Conor Kelly, 2025-11-04), then 'Programmatic Tool Calling' in 'Advanced tool use' (Bin Wu et al., 2025-11-24).

own-your-context-window.meaning: You do not need standard message-based formats to give context to an LLM. Own how the context is structured, for information density, error handling, safety, flexibility and token efficiency.
own-your-context-window.who: Dex Horthy (HumanLayer), Factor 3 of 12-Factor Agents. He recalls posting it around 2025-04-03.

needle-in-a-haystack.meaning: A long-context test that hides a fact (the needle) at varying depths in long filler text and asks the model to retrieve it, measuring recall across context lengths. It measures recall and fixes nothing. RULER calls it a superficial test, so passing it does not rule out context rot.

fighting-the-weights.meaning: The model will not do what you ask because you are working against its training. The warning signs are repeated instructions, ALL CAPS and pleading.
fighting-the-weights.who: Drew Breunig, 2025-11-11. Tim O'Reilly's write-up of Breunig's Foo Camp talk (2026-08-13) repeats it.
also_called: war-driving the thesaurus (escalating IMPORTANT, CRITICAL, MANDATORY)
fixed_by: validation and retry in the harness
reshaping the API to match what the model expects

page.label: Fighting the weights
page.text: Asking for something the model's training pulls against; repeating it louder doesn't help.

prompt-debt.meaning: The slowly accumulating cost of treating natural-language prompts as the specification of a system. Iteration slows, one-line hot fixes stop working, and the prompts tie you to a single model.
prompt-debt.who: No single coiner. The earliest use found is Ahmed Aljohani and Hyunsook Do, 'PromptDebt' (arXiv 2509.20497, 2025-09-24), in a different sense: self-admitted technical debt in prompt design. The hot-fix sense comes from Tian Pan ('prompt debt spiral', 2026-04-19) and Drew Breunig (2026-06-22, republished by O'Reilly Radar).
fixed_by: dead-clause audits (prune rules the model already follows)
specify tasks and let DSPy or GEPA find the wording

page.label: Prompt debt
page.text: Quick fixes pile up in a prompt until nobody dares touch it.

whack-a-mole.meaning: Prompt edits meant to fix specific failure modes often introduce equal and opposite regressions elsewhere, so performance plateaus.
whack-a-mole.who: An idiom, not coined by these authors. Applied to prompts by Simon Storf, Rich Barton-Cooper, James Peters-Gill and Marius Hobbhahn (arXiv 2603.00829, 2026-02-28, ICML 2026, Appendix F.3.1), in a paper on monitoring agents for scheming. Leech et al. (2024) used the idiom earlier for ad-hoc patching of models, a different sense.
fixed_by: limit manual prompt iterations (Storf et al. stopped at three)
prune and rewrite the prompt instead of appending

page.label: Whack-a-mole
page.text: Each prompt patch for one failure causes another somewhere else, and progress stalls.

instruction-stacking.meaning: What happens when a prompt accretes rules in response to bug reports without ever consolidating them. Tian Pan describes treating prompts 'like append-only configuration'.
instruction-stacking.who: Digital Applied Team (vendor blog, 2026-05-06). Tian Pan independently uses 'prompt sprawl' (2026-04-10).

prompt-bloat.meaning: Prompts or instruction files grow so big that they slow the model, burn context budget, or both. Anthropic: 'If your CLAUDE.md is too long, Claude ignores half of it because important rules get lost in the noise.'
prompt-bloat.who: 'The over-specified CLAUDE.md' is Anthropic's (Claude Code best-practices docs, undated). The origin of 'prompt bloat' is unknown. Its earliest fetched use is the title of the RAG-MCP paper (Gan and Sun, May 2025), and Redis (2025-07-15) calls it an architectural problem that a bigger window won't fix.
fixed_by: prune rules the model already follows

page.label: Prompt bloat
page.text: The prompt or instructions file grows so big that important rules get lost. Anthropic calls one form "the over-specified CLAUDE.md".

prompt-overfitting.meaning: Instructions or examples tuned on a small dev set score well there but worse on unseen inputs. In OPRO, training accuracy was often 5-20% above test accuracy.
prompt-overfitting.who: Borrowed from machine learning; no single coiner. Discussed for optimised prompts by Yang et al. (Google DeepMind, OPRO, arXiv 2309.03409, 2023), and applied to LLM-judge prompts by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar.
fixed_by: larger training set and fewer optimisation steps

page.label: Prompt overfitting
page.text: A prompt tuned on a few cases scores well there and worse everywhere else.

don-t-get-few-shotted.meaning: Language models are excellent mimics. A context full of similar action-observation pairs makes the agent keep copying that pattern even when it is no longer the best choice.
fixed_by: controlled variation in serialization, wording and ordering

majority-label-bias-recency-bias-common-.term: majority label bias, recency bias, common token bias
majority-label-bias-recency-bias-common-.meaning: In few-shot prompts, GPT-3 favours answers that are frequent in the prompt, answers near its end, and tokens common in pre-training. Accuracy swings from near chance to near state-of-the-art depending on example choice, order and format.
majority-label-bias-recency-bias-common-.who: Tony Z. Zhao, Eric Wallace, Shi Feng, Dan Klein, Sameer Singh, 'Calibrate Before Use' (ICML 2021, 2021-02-19).

anchoring-bias-in-llms.meaning: Initial information in the prompt disproportionately influences the model's judgment.
anchoring-bias-in-llms.who: Borrowed from cognitive psychology. Applied to LLMs by Jiaxu Lou and Yifan Sun (arXiv 2412.06593, 2024-12-09) and by Yiming Huang et al. (SynAnchors, 2025).

aggressive-prompt-language.meaning: Strongly worded instructions such as 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...' (Anthropic's term is 'aggressive language'). Newer models respond more strongly to the system prompt, so this wording makes them overtrigger.
aggressive-prompt-language.who: No common name. Anthropic's prompting docs call it 'aggressive language'. OpenAI's GPT-5 guide (Aug 2025, per search results) reports Cursor softening 'Be THOROUGH' wording.
fixed_by: normal wording plus the reason for the rule
emphasis only where an instruction is actually being skipped

page.label: Aggressive prompt language
page.text: "CRITICAL: you MUST…". Newer models follow the system prompt more closely, so shouting makes them over-trigger.

pink-elephant-problem.meaning: You instruct an LLM to avoid discussing a certain entity (the 'Pink Elephant') and to discuss a preferred one (the 'Grey Elephant') instead. Models find this hard to do reliably.
pink-elephant-problem.who: Louis Castricato, Nathan Lile, Suraj Anand, Hailey Schoelkopf, Siddharth Verma, Stella Biderman (arXiv 2402.07896, 2024-02-12), borrowing Wegner's white bear study (1987).
fixed_by: state what to do instead of what not to do

page.label: Pink Elephant problem
page.text: Telling a model not to mention something tends to bring it up.

prompt-drift.meaning: The model behind an API changes over time, so the same prompt may produce different results on the updated model.
prompt-drift.who: The Prompt Report attributes it to Chen et al. (2023b). Latitude (2026-07-20) separates drift (you changed nothing) from regression (a change you made made things worse).
also_called: instruction drift (third sense; see the context family)

page.label: Prompt drift
page.text: The same prompt behaves differently over time. People mean three things by it: the model changed, your own edits regressed it, or it fades over a long session.

sycophancy.meaning: Model responses that match the user's beliefs or please the user rather than being truthful. Human-feedback training can encourage this behaviour.
sycophancy.who: The term predates this work and its origin was not traced. Key measurement paper: Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong et al. (Anthropic, arXiv 2310.13548, 2023-10-20). Mainstream moment: OpenAI's GPT-4o rollback (2025-04-29). Coding-agent form: Claude Code issue #3382 (2025-07-12).
fixed_by: neutral prompt phrasing without your own opinion

page.label: Sycophancy
page.text: The model tells you what you want to hear instead of what is true.

overeagerness.meaning: The agent goes beyond the task. It creates extra files, unnecessary abstractions or flexibility nobody asked for, and adds tests, documentation, features or actions the user did not request.
overeagerness.who: No coinage. Documented by Anthropic: the 'Overeagerness' section of its Claude prompting docs, and the Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5 guides for unrequested additions. Also documented by Addy Osmani (2026-01-28).
also_called: scope creep (search handle, not a source term)
fixed_by: a minimal-solution prompt (scope, documentation, defensive coding, abstractions)
state the boundaries: mention extras at the end instead of doing them

page.label: Overeagerness
page.text: The agent goes beyond the task: extra files, extra abstractions, changes nobody asked for.

lobotomized.meaning: Community slang for a model that feels, or has been made, less capable, creative or personable after a release or over time. One sense is preference tuning (DPO/PPO) or abliteration pushed so far that the model gets worse. Another is restrictions added after launch, as with Bing Chat in 2023. Users usually blame safety tuning or cost cutting.
lobotomized.who: Unknown; community slang borrowing the brain-surgery metaphor. Uses read: an Ars Technica headline about Bing Chat with the word in scare quotes (2023-02-18, author unverified); Nathan Lambert (Interconnects, 2024-05-01); Maxime Labonne (2024-06-13); the Reddit post 'Opus 4.6 lobotomized' (2026-02-05, via Winbuzzer). None of them claims coinage.
fixed_by: light DPO to repair abliteration damage

alignment-tax.meaning: The extra cost of making an AI system aligned, compared with building an unaligned alternative. In LLM papers it usually means lost benchmark performance, or abilities the model forgot after alignment training such as RLHF.
alignment-tax.who: Paul Christiano credits the language to Eliezer Yudkowsky ('Current work in AI alignment', transcript 2020-04-03). Applied to LLM performance by Askell et al. (Anthropic, 2021-12) and Lin et al. (arXiv 2309.06256).
fixed_by: scale (Askell et al. find the tax small for large models)

exaggerated-safety.meaning: Models falsely refuse clearly safe prompts when those prompts use language similar to unsafe ones or mention sensitive topics. The authors trace this to lexical overfitting.
exaggerated-safety.who: Paul Röttger, Hannah Rose Kirk, Bertie Vidgen, Giuseppe Attanasio, Federico Bianchi, Dirk Hovy (XSTest, arXiv 2308.01263, 2023-08-02; NAACL 2024).

right-altitude.meaning: System prompts should sit in the Goldilocks zone between hardcoding complex, brittle logic and giving vague guidance that falsely assumes shared context. Prefer diverse, canonical examples over a laundry list of edge cases, and explain why a rule exists.
right-altitude.who: Anthropic Applied AI team (Rajasekaran, Dixon, Ryan, Hadfield), 2025-09-29.

page.label: Right altitude
page.text: The fix side: write instructions between brittle hard-coded rules and vague guidance.

role-prompting.meaning: Assigning a specific role (persona) to the model in the prompt, such as 'Madonna' or a travel writer.
role-prompting.who: Unknown. Zheng et al. (2023-11-16; EMNLP Findings 2024) found that personas do not improve accuracy on factual questions, and Basil et al. (2025-12-05) found the same. Anthropic still recommends a role for focus and tone.

reward-hacking.meaning: An AI fools its training or scoring process into giving it a high reward without completing the intended task. Examples are exploiting bugs in the scoring code, modifying the tests, or grabbing an existing answer.
reward-hacking.who: Used in the AI-safety literature since at least 'Concrete Problems in AI Safety' by Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt, Christiano, Schulman and Mané (arXiv 1606.06565, 2016-06-21). DeepMind's 'specification gaming' (2020) covers the same family. METR (2025-06-05) and Anthropic (2025-11-21) measured it in frontier coding agents.
also_called: specification gaming (older DeepMind term for the same family)

page.label: Reward hacking
page.text: The model games the score instead of doing the task.

special-casing-tests.meaning: Instead of implementing the general logic, a coding agent returns the expected test values or writes solutions that only work for the test inputs. It typically does this after several failed attempts at a real solution.
special-casing-tests.who: Anthropic: the Claude 3.7 Sonnet system card (section 6, per a secondary summary; the card itself was not read), the Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card, and the Claude prompting docs.
also_called: passing tests at the expense of general solutions
fixed_by: a prompt asking for a general solution and to flag incorrect tests instead of working around them

page.label: Special-casing tests
page.text: The agent hard-codes the expected test values instead of writing the real logic.

declaring-the-job-done-prematurely.meaning: An agent marks a feature or task as done without testing it end to end, or declares the whole job done because it sees that some progress has been made.
declaring-the-job-done-prematurely.who: No coinage. Descriptive wording used only by Anthropic, across several docs: Justin Young's long-running harness post (2025-11-26), the Claude Code best practices, and the Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5 guides.
fixed_by: audit each progress claim against a tool result

page.label: Declaring done too early
page.text: The agent marks the task done without testing it end to end.

laziness.meaning: A model leaves a task incomplete or gives thinner, briefer output than asked for. OpenAI described 'cases of laziness where the model doesn't complete a task.'
laziness.who: ChatGPT users. OpenAI's @ChatGPTapp account acknowledged it (2023-12-08).

doom-loop.meaning: Going round in circles trying to get an LLM to fix a problem it cannot solve. Vendors and bloggers also use it for an agent repeating the same error across sessions, or spiralling through blind fixes without running the code.
doom-loop.who: Unknown; no primary coinage found. The earliest use read is Jason Gorman's post (dated 2025-09-30, but the version read was updated 2026-04-14). Other senses: Unblocked (vendor, 2026-04-18) and HackerNoon (2026-06-26). Anthropic's name for the human side is 'Correcting over and over'.
fixed_by: persist corrections in CLAUDE.md or skills

page.label: Doom loop
page.text: Going round in circles asking the agent to fix something it can't.

package-hallucination.meaning: A code-generating LLM recommends or imports a software package that does not exist, an error attackers can exploit as a package confusion attack. The rate is at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones.
package-hallucination.who: First named 'AI package hallucination' by Bar Lanyado and Vulcan Cyber's Voyager18 team (2023-06-06, per Infosecurity Magazine). Systematic study by Spracklen et al. (arXiv 2406.10279, USENIX Security 2025), who did not coin the term.

page.label: Package hallucination
page.text: The agent imports a package that doesn't exist.

evals.meaning: An eval is a test for an AI system: give the AI an input, then apply grading logic to its output to measure success.
evals.who: No single coiner. OpenAI open-sourced its Evals framework on 2023-03-14. Hamel Husain popularised product-specific evals (2024-03-29). The quoted definition is Anthropic's (2026-01-09).
fixes: real context size (claimed versus effective context length)

page.label: Evals
page.text: Tests for AI behaviour: an input, the output, and grading logic.

error-analysis.meaning: Read real traces and write open-ended notes on failures (open coding). Then group the notes into a failure taxonomy and count per category (axial coding), so you know which evals are worth writing.
error-analysis.who: Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, for the open/axial-coding method in their evals FAQ. They did not coin the generic phrase.
fixes: generic metrics that create false confidence

page.label: Error analysis
page.text: Read real traces, note each failure, group the notes into categories and count them, so you know which evals are worth writing.

eval-driven-development.meaning: Evaluations serve as the working specification for an LLM-powered application. They are written before or alongside the feature and used to gate every change (Braintrust). Anthropic describes writing evals for capabilities the agent cannot yet handle, then iterating until it can.
eval-driven-development.who: Unknown. The earliest verified use is Vercel (2024-10-17). Later: Husain and Shankar (2025-07-27, critical: 'Generally no'), Anthropic (2026-01-09), Braintrust (2026-02-18).

llm-as-a-judge.meaning: Using a strong LLM to evaluate other models' or agents' outputs on open-ended tasks, as a cheap, scalable stand-in for human preference judgments.
llm-as-a-judge.who: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng et al., 'Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena' (arXiv 2306.05685, 2023-06-09; NeurIPS 2023).

page.label: LLM-as-a-judge
page.text: A strong model grades another model's or agent's output.

generator-evaluator-loop.meaning: A separate evaluator agent, tuned to be skeptical, grades the generator agent's work. This is needed because agents asked to grade their own output tend to praise it confidently even when it is mediocre.
generator-evaluator-loop.who: Anthropic. 'Building effective agents' (Erik Schluntz, Barry Zhang, 2024-12-19) calls it the 'evaluator-optimizer' workflow. Prithvi Rajasekaran extended it into a planner/generator/evaluator harness (2026-03-24), and the Claude Code docs name the 'Writer/Reviewer pattern'.

page.label: Generator and evaluator
page.text: A second, sceptical agent grades the first agent's work.

tdd-with-agents.meaning: The agent writes tests first, confirms they fail, then iterates on the implementation until they pass. Without this, agents tend to produce broken or unused code and regressions.
tdd-with-agents.who: No coiner. Kent Beck described it (Pragmatic Engineer 2025-06-11; 'Augmented Coding: Beyond the Vibes' 2025-06-25), and Simon Willison named the 'Red/green TDD' pattern. Beck warns that agents delete tests to make them 'pass'.

page.label: TDD with agents
page.text: The agent writes failing tests first, then works until they pass.

backpressure.meaning: Automated feedback around an agent that lets it find and fix its own mistakes as it goes, instead of a human doing so: build tools, type systems, compiler errors, linters, tests, browser or DevTools MCP servers. The human-side sense is the time you spend giving feedback the agent could have gotten itself.
backpressure.who: Geoffrey Huntley first used it for agents (Ralph post, 2025-07-14). Moss (banay.me, 2026-01-17) wrote the definition people quote. Both come from the same circle.
also_called: sensors (Böckeler's word for the same idea)

page.label: Backpressure
page.text: Builds, types, linters and tests that let the agent catch its own mistakes before you have to.

plan-mode.meaning: A mode in which the agent researches the codebase and proposes changes or a plan, and edits no source files until the human approves the plan. Distinct from the plan-then-execute security pattern.
plan-mode.who: No single coiner. Cline's Plan/Act toggle came around 2025-01 (Saoud Rizwan claims it was first). Claude Code plan mode followed on 2025-06-11 (Boris Cherny), and Cursor Plan Mode on 2025-10-07 (Jai Smith).

page.label: Plan mode
page.text: The agent researches and proposes a plan, and nothing is edited until you approve it.

spec-driven-development.meaning: Write a structured, behaviour-oriented spec before the AI writes code, and treat it as the source of truth for both human and AI. Böckeler's loose definition is 'documentation first'.
spec-driven-development.who: Unknown; Böckeler calls the term 'semantically diffused'. Main early sources: Kiro (AWS, 2025-07-14), Sean Grove's 'The New Code' talk (OpenAI, 2025), GitHub Spec Kit (Den Delimarsky, 2025-09-02).

page.label: Spec-driven development
page.text: Write a structured spec first and treat it as the source of truth for you and the agent. The meaning is still loose.

prompt-injection.meaning: A security exploit in which untrusted input joined into a prompt makes the model follow the attacker's instructions instead of the developer's. It is named by analogy with SQL injection.
prompt-injection.who: Simon Willison named it (2022-09-12) and credits Riley Goodside with first demonstrating the attack. Indirect prompt injection: Greshake et al. (2023-02-23).
also_called: indirect prompt injection (payload in fetched content)

page.label: Prompt injection
page.text: Untrusted text in the prompt makes the model follow the attacker instead of you.

lethal-trifecta.meaning: An attacker can trick an agent into stealing your data if the agent combines three things: access to your private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally.
fixed_by: remove one of the three legs

page.label: Lethal trifecta
page.text: An agent with private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out can be tricked into leaking it.

jailbreaking.meaning: The process of getting a GenAI model to do or say unintended things through prompting (The Prompt Report §5.1.1).
jailbreaking.who: Unknown. Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt (NeurIPS 2023) analyse why safety training fails, through 'competing objectives' and 'mismatched generalization'. OWASP treats it as a subset of prompt injection; Willison treats the two as different problems.

slopsquatting.meaning: An attacker registers a non-existent package name that LLMs hallucinate, hoping a developer following an AI assistant installs the fake package without noticing. It exploits package hallucination.
slopsquatting.who: Seth Larson (Python Software Foundation), per Socket (2025-04-08). Popularised by Andrew Nesbitt. The attribution chain is secondary.

page.label: Slopsquatting
page.text: Attackers register package names that models tend to hallucinate.

agent-harness.meaning: Every piece of code, configuration and execution logic that is not the model itself, summed up as 'Agent = Model + Harness'. Not to be confused with an evaluation harness or a test harness.
agent-harness.who: No single coiner. The earliest dated uses read are Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK post (Thariq Shihipar, 2025-09-29) and 'Effective harnesses for long-running agents' (Justin Young, 2025-11-26), then Philipp Schmid (2026-01-05). The formula is Vivek Trivedy's at LangChain (2026-03-10).

page.label: Agent harness
page.text: Everything around the model: tools, instructions, hooks, loop. "Agent = model + harness."

harness-engineering.meaning: In Hashimoto's sense: every time an agent errs, engineer a fix (an AGENTS.md rule or a purpose-built tool or script) so that it never makes that mistake again. OpenAI and Böckeler use it more broadly, for building the whole environment of scaffolding, guides, sensors and feedback loops around the agent.
harness-engineering.who: Nobody claims it. The earliest use found is Mitchell Hashimoto (2026-02-05), who disclaims inventing a term. OpenAI's Ryan Lopopolo made it widely known with 'Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world' (2026-02-11); that page was not fetched.

page.label: Harness engineering
page.text: Every time the agent makes a mistake, add a rule, tool or check so it can't happen again.

agent-loop.meaning: An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal. The model asks its harness to act, the results go back to the model, and this continues until a stopping condition is met.
agent-loop.who: No single coiner. Josh Bickett's 2023-11 meme 'An LLM in a loop with an objective', then Anthropic (2024-12-19), then Simon Willison's wording (2025-09-18).

page.label: Agent loop
page.text: A model running tools in a loop until a goal is met.

agent-computer-interface.meaning: A purpose-built interface between an LM agent and the computer: the commands the agent can use and the format of the feedback it receives. It is designed for the agent as a new category of end user, not for humans.
agent-computer-interface.who: John Yang, Carlos E. Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, Ofir Press (Princeton), SWE-agent paper (arXiv 2405.15793, 2024-05-06). Adopted in Anthropic's 'Building effective agents'.

guardrails.meaning: Runtime checks around an LLM application that control its behaviour. NeMo's wording: 'a specific way of controlling the output of an LLM', such as avoiding harmful topics or following a set dialogue path. The word is vague, so name the actual mechanism when precision matters.
guardrails.who: A generic engineering word. NVIDIA (Traian Rebedea, Razvan Dinu, Makesh Sreedhar, Christopher Parisien, Jonathan Cohen) popularised 'programmable rails' with NeMo Guardrails (arXiv 2310.10501, 2023-10-16). The OpenAI Agents SDK adds input, output and tool guardrails with tripwires.

page.label: Guardrails
page.text: Runtime checks around an AI app. Vague across vendors: name the mechanism when it matters.

hooks.meaning: User-defined shell commands that Claude Code runs at fixed points in its lifecycle; handlers can now also be HTTP endpoints, MCP tools, prompts or subagents. They give deterministic control: certain actions always happen, rather than depending on the LLM choosing to run them. CLAUDE.md is only advisory, whereas a Stop hook can block the turn from ending until a check passes.
hooks.who: A generic word. Anthropic's Claude Code docs popularised hooks as deterministic guardrails. The meaning differs by tool: Kiro hooks are event-driven automations on file save, and LangChain treats hooks and middleware as harness parts.

page.label: Hooks
page.text: Commands that run at fixed points in the agent's lifecycle. They are deterministic, so use them for rules that must always hold.

sandboxing.meaning: Running the agent inside pre-defined boundaries, so it can work freely without damaging the host or leaking data. Anthropic says this needs both filesystem isolation (only specific directories) and network isolation (only approved servers).
sandboxing.who: A generic security term. The agent-specific sources are Simon Willison, 'Designing agentic loops' (2025-09-30), and Anthropic's Claude Code sandboxing post (David Dworken, Oliver Weller-Davies, 2025-10-20), which self-reports 84% fewer permission prompts.

page.label: Sandboxing
page.text: The agent runs inside fixed walls (files, network) so it can work freely without harm.
page.named_by: Security term; Anthropic, Willison for agents

ai-boxing.meaning: Confining a powerful AI, literally or metaphorically, so that it can affect the wider world only through restricted channels, often a human liaison. This can be physical containment or restriction of the information going in and out. It is an AI-safety term, not a prompt-engineering practice.
ai-boxing.who: Eliezer Yudkowsky's 'AI-Box Experiment' (two runs in 2002) popularised the idea of a box, though his page never uses the word 'boxing'. 'Boxing methods' appears in Armstrong, Sandberg and Bostrom (2012) and in Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014), under capability control. Nobody verified who first said 'AI boxing'.

agents-rule-of-two.meaning: Until prompt injection can be reliably detected and refused, an agent may have no more than two of these three properties within a session: it processes untrustworthy inputs, it has access to sensitive systems or private data, and it can change state or communicate externally.
agents-rule-of-two.who: Meta AI blog (2025-10-31), with no named authors; Willison says Mick Ayzenberg shared it. Inspired by Chromium's Rule of 2 and Willison's lethal trifecta.

page.label: Agents Rule of Two
page.text: In one session, an agent may have at most two of three: untrusted input, sensitive access, outside actions.

dual-llm-pattern.meaning: A privileged LLM sees only trusted input and can use tools. A quarantined LLM handles untrusted content and has no tools. Ordinary code passes the quarantined output around as opaque variables and never forwards it unfiltered to the privileged model.

plan-then-execute.meaning: The agent first commits to a fixed list of actions, so tool outputs cannot influence which actions it takes, a protection likened to control-flow integrity. Distinct from plan mode.
plan-then-execute.who: Beurer-Kellner, Buesser, Cretu, Debenedetti, Dobos, Fabian, Fischer, Froelicher, Grosse, Naeff, Ozoani, Paverd, Tramèr and Volhejn, 'Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections' (arXiv 2506.08837, 2025-06-10).

instruction-hierarchy.meaning: A priority ordering over instruction sources that the model is trained to follow when they conflict, so that it selectively ignores lower-privileged instructions.
instruction-hierarchy.who: Eric Wallace, Kai Xiao, Reimar Leike, Lilian Weng, Johannes Heidecke, Alex Beutel (OpenAI), arXiv 2404.13208, 2024-04-19.

least-privilege-for-agents.meaning: Every program and privileged user should operate with the least privilege necessary (Saltzer). For LLM agents, OWASP applies this by keeping tools, extension functionality and permissions to the minimum necessary, running actions in the user's context, and requiring human approval for high-impact actions.
least-privilege-for-agents.who: Jerome Saltzer (CACM, 1974, per Wikipedia), popularised by Saltzer and Schroeder (1975). Applied to LLM agents by OWASP LLM06:2025 'Excessive Agency'. Auth0 attributes 'least agency' to OWASP's Agentic Top 10, a secondary attribution.
also_called: excessive agency (OWASP LLM06, the failure mode)

page.label: Least privilege
page.text: Give the agent only the access the task needs.

human-in-the-loop.meaning: A human must instigate or approve the system's consequential actions before they happen. OWASP's wording for LLM agents: 'require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken'. Its known failure mode is approval fatigue.
human-in-the-loop.who: The phrase is older and has no single coiner. Wikipedia credits the in/on/out-of-the-loop taxonomy to Bonnie Docherty, Human Rights Watch, 'Losing Humanity' (2012-11-19). Adopted for agents by OWASP, Anthropic and Meta.
fixes: lethal trifecta tasks that need all three properties (Meta requires human approval)

page.label: Human in the loop
page.text: A person approves consequential actions before they happen. "On the loop": a person watches and can stop it.

human-on-the-loop.meaning: The system acts on its own under the oversight of a human operator who can override or abort its actions.
human-on-the-loop.who: Bonnie Docherty, Human Rights Watch, 'Losing Humanity' (2012-11-19), per Wikipedia. The LLM-agent sense was seen only in vendor posts that were not fetched.

yolo-mode.meaning: Running a coding agent where everything is approved by default. Willison calls it 'so dangerous, but also key to getting the most productive results'. Claude Code docs say bypassPermissions is for 'isolated containers and VMs only'.
yolo-mode.who: Unknown. It was Cursor's feature name by 2024-12-20 (later renamed auto-run). Simon Willison generalised it as 'what I like to call YOLO mode' (2025-09-30).
fixes: approval fatigue (the reason people turn it on; safe only inside a sandbox)

page.label: YOLO mode
page.text: Everything approved by default. Every source says: only inside a sandbox.
