ralph-wiggum-technique.meaning: In its purest form, a Bash loop, `while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done`, that feeds the same prompt to a coding agent over and over. Each loop does one task in a new context window, so progress lives in files and git rather than in the context.
ralph-wiggum-technique.who: Geoffrey Huntley, 'Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer', 2025-07-14. Anthropic's ralph-wiggum plugin credits him, but it runs inside one session through a Stop hook, so it does not get a fresh window per iteration.

page.label: Ralph loop
page.text: Feed the same prompt to a coding agent again and again. Each round does one task in a fresh context; progress lives in files and git.

guides-and-sensors.meaning: Guides anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts: AGENTS.md, skills, language servers, codemods. Sensors observe after it acts and help it self-correct: linters, tests, type checkers, AI review. You need both.
guides-and-sensors.who: Birgitta Böckeler, martinfowler.com (2026-04-02). An earlier memo of 2026-02-17 was not checked.
fixes: rules with no way to know if they worked (feedforward alone)

vibe-coding.meaning: Karpathy's term for fully giving in to the vibes and forgetting the code exists: accept all changes, don't read the diffs, paste errors back and see what works. Willison narrows it to building software with an LLM without reviewing the code it writes.
vibe-coding.who: Andrej Karpathy, in a post on X dated 2025-02-02 per Sarkar and Drosos and the tweet ID. Willison's 'February 6th' conflicts with this.

page.label: Vibe coding
page.text: Accept everything, don't read the diffs, paste errors back and see what works.

ai-slop.meaning: Unreviewed, mindlessly generated AI content pushed on someone who did not ask for it, named by analogy with spam. For code, the equivalent is 'inflicting unreviewed code on collaborators'.
ai-slop.who: In-group slang from about 2022 (4chan, Hacker News, YouTube, per Wikipedia). Popularised by Simon Willison (2024-05-08), crediting a tweet by @deepfates. Merriam-Webster and the American Dialect Society chose 'slop' as their 2025 Word of the Year.
fixed_by: review the code before sharing it

page.label: AI slop
page.text: Unreviewed AI output pushed on people who didn't ask for it.

comprehension-debt.meaning: The gap that builds when teams produce code faster than they can understand it. Gorman frames it as the extra time needed to understand code before it can be safely changed. Storey frames it as the erosion of a team's shared understanding of how and why the system works.
comprehension-debt.who: 'Comprehension debt': Jason Gorman (Codemanship, 2025-09-30), popularised by Addy Osmani; several secondary sources wrongly credit Osmani. 'Cognitive debt': the phrase comes from MIT Media Lab's 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' (Kosmyna et al., 2025-06-10, a study of essay writing). Margaret-Anne Storey gave it the software sense (2026-02-09) without claiming the term.
also_called: cognitive debt (Storey; Osmani treats the two as interchangeable)
triple debt model (technical, cognitive and intent debt)

page.label: Comprehension debt
page.text: The team ships code faster than it can understand it.

cognitive-surrender.meaning: Adopting AI-generated outputs with minimal scrutiny or insufficient verification, so that the AI's answer becomes your own. It is contrasted with cognitive offloading, where you hand the method to a tool but still judge the result.
cognitive-surrender.who: Steven D. Shaw and Gideon Nave (Wharton), 'Thinking—Fast, Slow, and Artificial' (SSRN working paper, 2026). The paper itself was not read, only the SSRN interview of 2026-07-13. Addy Osmani applied it to coding (2026-05-05).
fixed_by: cognitive offloading instead: keep forming an independent view

automation-bias.meaning: The tendency of users to over-value salient automated cues even when more reliable information is available.
automation-bias.who: A human-factors term from 1990s aviation research: Mosier, Skitka, Heers and Burdick, 'Automation Bias: Decision Making and Performance in High-Tech Cockpits' (cited as 1997), and Mosier and Skitka (1999). Gardella, Bolton and Riggs (2026-04-21) invoke it for AI code generation.

page.label: Automation bias
page.text: Trusting the machine's answer over better information you already have.

skill-atrophy.meaning: Skills decline or are lost over time from lack of use or practice, here because thinking and coding are delegated to AI. Anthropic's randomised trial found that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging.
skill-atrophy.who: A generic term. Addy Osmani applied it to AI coding (2025-04-25). Anthropic researchers Judy Hanwen Shen and Alex Tamkin measured the effect under the name skill formation (arXiv 2601.20245, 2026-01-28).
fixed_by: coding without the agent on a schedule

page.label: Skill atrophy
page.text: Skills fade because the thinking is always delegated.

70-problem.meaning: Non-engineers using AI coding tools get 70% of the way surprisingly quickly, but the final 30% becomes an exercise in diminishing returns.
70-problem.who: Addy Osmani, 2024-12-04. It is an anecdotal framing, not a measurement.

page.label: 70% problem
page.text: AI gets non-engineers 70% of the way fast; the last 30% turns into diminishing returns.

babysitting-the-agent.meaning: Spending most of your time watching, redirecting and correcting agents rather than coding. As one developer put it: 'You're not coding anymore, you're supervising.'
babysitting-the-agent.who: Unknown. Addy Osmani (2026-01-28) quotes a Hacker News commenter: 'I spend most of my time babysitting agents.'

approval-fatigue.meaning: After clicking through many permission prompts, people stop paying close attention to what they are approving. Anthropic measured that users accept 93% of permission prompts.
approval-fatigue.who: No coiner; a generic security-UX term. The earliest agent-specific use found is Anthropic, 'Beyond permission prompts' (David Dworken, Oliver Weller-Davies, 2025-10-20). Later uses: Anthropic's auto mode post (John Hughes, 2026-03-25) and WorkOS (2026-08).

page.label: Approval fatigue
page.text: After many permission prompts, people stop reading what they approve.

token-maxxing.grade_note: as workplace slang: Wikipedia, WSJ, Forbes, Business Insider, Axios and The Pragmatic Engineer use it the same way; no coiner
token-maxxing.meaning: Treating how many AI tokens a person burns as a measure of how productive they are, usually through company leaderboards of agent usage. People then game the number: Microsoft engineers described asking the AI 'to prototype a feature that I have no intention of working on' and defaulting to the agent 'even when I know I could do the work by hand much faster'. Orosz compares it to the discredited lines-of-code metric; Wikipedia links it to Goodhart's law.
token-maxxing.who: No known coiner. The earliest dated uses Wikipedia cites are Forbes (Richard Nieva, 2026-03-31) and Forbes (Tim Keary, 2026-04-13, the first 'tokenmaxxing' headline); those two were not fetched. The '-maxx' suffix is internet slang. Gergely Orosz (The Pragmatic Engineer, 2026-04-23) reports, via The Information, Meta's 'Claudeonomics' leaderboard: over 85,000 employees, 60.2 trillion tokens in 30 days, 'Massive waste', then abolished. Microsoft has had a token leaderboard since January 2026; Salesforce set weekly minimum spend targets ($100 on Claude Code); Shopify renamed its leaderboard 'usage dashboard'. Also covered by WSJ, Business Insider and Axios, and used in an arXiv title (Wu, Anderson, Guha, 2026-07-24).
fixed_by: judge outcomes, not token counts (Orosz: the lines-of-code mistake again)
usage dashboard instead of a leaderboard (Shopify)
circuit breakers to catch runaway agents (Shopify)

page.label: Token maxxing
page.text: Counting tokens burned as a measure of productivity, often on a leaderboard. People game it, and it repeats the old lines-of-code mistake.
page.named_by: No single author, 2026; Meta, Microsoft and Salesforce tracked it

meat-proxy.grade_note: slang with a defining source; widely repeated since 2026-08
meat-proxy.meaning: A person who passes AI output on to colleagues without reading, understanding or checking it: 'Claude said:' followed by the pasted answer. Gruhn: 'I don't need a meat proxy in between.' In code: the ticket goes to the agent, the diff goes to review unread, reviewer comments go back to the agent. 'But who has done the implementation? The reviewers did, using Claude Code, and you as a meat proxy.'
meat-proxy.who: First used by Frank Allenby, 'meat-based llm proxies' (not-an-llm blog, 2026-03-31). His page was down (HTTP 530) when checked; the credit comes from sf-isms ('Coined by: Frank Allenby') and Simon Willison's correction. Made popular by Niklas Gruhn, 'Don't be a meat proxy' (2026-08-03, Hacker News front page); Gruhn does not claim to have coined it. Willison linked it the same day ('an excellent new term') and later added Allenby's earlier use. Business Insider and the BBC covered it, per search results not fetched.
fixed_by: read it, understand it, validate it, then answer in your own words (Gruhn)
own the diff: read it before you ask anyone to review it

page.label: Meat proxy
page.text: Passing the agent's answer to colleagues without reading it: "Claude said:" plus the paste, or a diff sent to review that you never read. The reviewers end up doing the engineering.
page.named_by: Frank Allenby, March 2026; made popular by Niklas Gruhn, August 2026

agentic-engineering.meaning: Professional agent-assisted development: the AI does the implementation while the human owns architecture, quality and correctness. Osmani: 'Vibe coding = YOLO. Agentic engineering = AI does the implementation, human owns the architecture, quality, and correctness.'
agentic-engineering.who: Andrej Karpathy suggested the name around 2026-02-04, per Osmani; Karpathy's own post was not read. Simon Willison independently used 'vibe engineering' for the same idea from 2025-10-07, and noted in 2026-02 that 'agentic engineering' had become more popular.
also_called: vibe engineering (Willison's earlier name for the same idea)

page.label: Agentic engineering
page.text: The professional version: the agent implements, the engineer owns architecture, quality and correctness.

cognitive-offloading.grade_note: cognitive psychology since 2016; for AI its meaning is split: healthy delegation or over-reliance
cognitive-offloading.meaning: Using a tool or an action to cut the thinking a task needs: a phone reminder, a calculator, now an AI. Risko and Gilbert: 'the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand.' Shaw: 'Cognitive offloading is strategic delegation. You remain in control of the decision, but you choose to offload a specific component of cognition to AI.' It is a move only in that sense; many AI papers use the same words for the harmful kind (see caveats).
cognitive-offloading.who: Evan F. Risko and Sam J. Gilbert, 'Cognitive Offloading', Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20(9):676-688 (2016). Steven D. Shaw and Gideon Nave (Wharton, SSRN working paper 2026; interview 2026-07-13) set it against cognitive surrender. AI-education papers often use it for over-reliance instead, e.g. Aiersilan, 'The Vibe-Check Protocol: Quantifying Cognitive Offloading in AI Programming' (arXiv 2601.02410, 2026-01-02), which contrasts students 'leveraging AI for acceleration versus those using it for cognitive offloading'.
fixes: cognitive surrender (only while you keep the decision)

page.label: Cognitive offloading
page.text: Handing one piece of the thinking to a tool while you keep the decision, like a calculator or a reminder. Healthy in this sense; see below for the other one.

counts_for.says: You asked {n} side questions with /btw in {chats} sessions.
You started {n} forked sub-agents with /subtask or /btw, in {chats} sessions.
You @-mentioned a sub-agent by name {n} times in {chats} sessions.
You set a goal with /goal {n} times in {chats} sessions.
You set a goal with /goal {n} times in {chats} sessions.
You asked for a plan with /plan {n} times in {chats} sessions.
